43019503.title: Second Cancer Risk in Female Survivors of Hodgkin Lymphoma: A National Cohort Analysis Across Treatment Eras.
43019503.author: Macklin-Doherty A
43019503.abstract:
PURPOSE: Subsequent primary malignancies (SPMs) are the leading cause of long-term treatment-related mortality in Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). Although treatments have evolved substantially over recent decades, few studies have demonstrated reductions in SPM risks following modern treatments, nor how such changes should inform survivorship care and screening. We analyzed SPM risks in a large female cohort of childhood and adult patients with HL treated over a 60-year period.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This population-based cohort study included 7,428 women diagnosed with HL before age 36 years in England and Wales from 1954 to 2010, with follow-up through 2018. SPMs were ascertained via national cancer registry linkages. Standardized incidence ratios (SIRs), absolute excess risks, and multivariable models were used to assess temporal trends and associations with treatment.
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 20.2 years, 1,200 women developed 1,467 invasive cancers (SIR, 3.3 [95% CI, 3.1 to 3.5]), most commonly breast, lung, and thyroid cancers. Solid tumor risks were the highest following radiotherapy, with a strong dose-dependent response. Alkylator use with radiotherapy was associated with reduced risks of breast cancer but increased risks of GI cancers. Solid cancer risks decreased by 25% between treatment periods 1954-1989 and 2000-2010. The decrease was attenuated and nonsignificant after adjustment for radiotherapy but not affected by adjustment for chemotherapy. No decline was observed for hematologic malignancies. Cumulative incidence of SPMs reached 36% at 50 years.
CONCLUSION: Female patients treated in more recent eras have a substantially lower long-term risk of solid SPMs largely attributable to the reduced use, dose, and improvement in radiotherapy. Nevertheless, persistently elevated risks remained beyond 50 years of follow-up, particularly for lung and breast cancer, underscoring the need for lifelong surveillance and targeted screening of survivors.

43013351.title: Palbociclib, Fulvestrant, Trastuzumab, and Pyrotinib for Patients with Advanced Breast Cancer with Brain Metastases: A Prospective Multicenter Phase 2 Trial.
43013351.author: Chen D
43013351.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-positive (HER2+) advanced breast cancer (ABC) face a high risk of brain metastases (BMs), yet prospective systemic‑treatment evidence for this subgroup is limited. We conducted a multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 trial evaluating a chemotherapy-sparing regimen of palbociclib, fulvestrant, trastuzumab, and pyrotinib in patients with HR+/HER2+ ABC and measurable BMs. The interim analysis suggested preliminary intracranial activity with manageable toxicity.
METHODS: Eligible patients had HR+/HER2+ ABC with measurable BMs and no prior local treatment to the target lesion. The regimen was administered until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or death. The primary endpoint was confirmed central nervous system objective response rate (CNS-ORR). Secondary endpoints included overall ORR, progression-free survival (PFS), CNS-PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. We present the final analysis for 32 enrolled patients.
RESULTS: From Dec 2020 to Feb 2026, 32 patients were enrolled. For 29 response‑evaluable patients, confirmed CNS‑ORR was 58.6% (95%CI 40.7‑74.5) and overall ORR 62.1% (95%CI 44.0‑77.3). With median follow‑up of 32.5 months, median CNS-PFS was 9.6 months (95% CI: 5.3-13.9), and median overall PFS was 12.3 months (95% CI: 6.8-17.7). OS remained immature (5 deaths; 24‑month‑OS rate 80.7%). Post‑hoc analyses suggested numerically better PFS/CNS‑PFS in chemotherapy‑naïve patients, whereas prior trastuzumab did not impair efficacy. Frequent grade ≥3 adverse events comprised diarrhea (37.5%), neutropenia (28.1%) and leukopenia (15.6%), with no treatment‑related deaths.
CONCLUSIONS: The chemotherapy-sparing quadruple regimen showed promising intracranial activity, systemic disease control, and manageable toxicity in HR+/HER2+ ABC patients with BMs.

43024835.title: Clinician Competencies for Self-Management Support in Cancer: Expert Consensus Recommendations From the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer.
43024835.author: Knowles R
43024835.abstract:
PURPOSE: Many people affected by cancer benefit from self-management, but this requires support from cancer care clinicians. Currently, there is a lack of consensus about the minimum competencies required of clinicians to facilitate effective self-management support (SMS).
METHODS: A two-round online modified Delphi study involving cancer care clinicians was conducted to reach consensus on which performance criteria from a comprehensive SMS framework for cancer nurses should be considered minimum competencies that cancer care clinicians should possess. The perspectives of people affected by cancer regarding SMS needs were collected via online interviews and further shaped the statements. The project team finalized a list of minimum competencies for care-providers (care-provider version) and a reader-adjusted version for people affected by cancer (patient version).
RESULTS: 27 clinicians and 14 people affected by cancer participated. Eighteen performance criteria from the original framework reached consensus for inclusion as minimum competencies, with participant feedback informing refinements to both the care-provider and patient versions. The performance criteria included statements from all six domains of the original framework: person-centered and motivational communication, whole-person assessment of SMS needs and capacity, health promotion theories and interventions, coaching for behavior change tailored to the individual, monitoring and evaluating change in self-management behaviors and health outcomes, and quality improvement for integration of SMS in cancer care.
CONCLUSION: The minimum competencies for SMS can be used to inform care provider education, skills assessment, and encourage patient activation for improved support, to optimize patient outcomes and health care utilization. International organizations, such as the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer, represent an ideal forum for the dissemination and strengthening of these competencies, and for local implementation.

43020098.title: Lynch syndrome.
43020098.author: Ryan NAJ
43020098.abstract: Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited cancer predisposition syndrome, affecting approximately one in 350-450 individuals, yet the majority of carriers remain undiagnosed, representing a substantial and preventable public health burden. Caused by germline pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, Lynch syndrome confers markedly elevated and heterogeneous risks of colorectal, endometrial, and multiple extracolonic cancers. Advances in molecular diagnostics, particularly universal tumour testing for MMR deficiency, have transformed case identification and enabled targeted germline testing and cascade screening of relatives at risk. Despite these advances, implementation remains inconsistent, with substantial attrition across diagnostic pathways and inequities in access to care. Preventive strategies-including colonoscopic surveillance, aspirin chemoprevention, and risk-reducing surgery-are effective but require gene-specific and individualised application. Therapeutically, the immunogenic biology of MMR-deficient tumours has positioned Lynch syndrome at the forefront of precision oncology, with immune checkpoint inhibitors delivering substantial benefit and emerging vaccine strategies offering promise for cancer interception. In this Review, we provide an integrated overview of Lynch syndrome across the continuum of care, highlighting advances in biology, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment, while emphasising the crucial need to align scientific progress with equitable and effective health-system delivery.

43008246.title: From Assessment to Action: Integrating Patient-Reported Concerns Into Routine Breast Cancer Survivorship Care.
43008246.author: Rosenberg C
43008246.abstract:
PURPOSE: Breast cancer survivorship care requires systematic approaches to identify and address patient-identified needs after completion of treatment.
METHODS: Breast cancer survivors completing curative-intent treatment were referred to a risk-adapted survivorship program incorporating a structured previsit patient-reported concerns assessment. Descriptive analyses characterized the prevalence and longitudinal consistency of survivor-reported concerns. Aggregated concerns data supported real-time clinical decision making during survivorship visits and informed program-level planning, including alignment of consultative services and survivorship education embedded within routine oncology care.
RESULTS: Two thousand five hundred fifty-eight breast cancer survivors completed the previsit patient-reported concerns assessment during survivorship visits from 2019 through 2025. Survivors reported a consistent set of physical, psychosocial, and lifestyle-related concerns across the study period. These survivor-identified concerns informed referral to established consultative services and guided development of survivorship education aligned with survivor-identified needs. Concern patterns were reviewed longitudinally to support alignment of survivorship services and education with evolving survivor priorities.
CONCLUSION: Integration of structured patient-reported concerns into routine survivorship care is feasible and supports responsive, patient-centered care delivery. This pragmatic approach may inform scalable, real-world implementation of survivorship program models without disrupting existing clinical workflows.

43006918.title: Advancing gastric cancer prevention in the United States: perspectives from a congressional forum.
43006918.author: Hyun CS
43006918.abstract: Effective strategies for gastric cancer prevention and early detection are available, yet they are not consistently implemented in the United States, particularly among populations at increased risk. As a result, many patients continue to be diagnosed with advanced disease despite opportunities for earlier intervention. A recent Congressional Forum brought together clinicians, researchers, patient advocates, and policymakers to examine barriers to translating established gastric cancer prevention strategies into routine practice. Integrating perspectives presented during the forum with published evidence and current clinical guidance, this Commentary presents a multidisciplinary, implementation-oriented policy framework addressing the clinical, informational, organizational, and access barriers that contribute to delayed diagnosis. Established approaches, including Helicobacter pylori testing and treatment, endoscopic detection of premalignant gastric lesions, and risk-based clinical assessment, provide a strong foundation for prevention but remain underused in routine practice. Building on this foundation, we propose practical policy priorities to improve implementation, including integration of gastric cancer risk assessment into routine clinical evaluation, incorporation of electronic health record based clinical decision support, and development of coordinated pathways for risk-based testing, referral, and surveillance. Advancing a national strategy that aligns prevention, clinical practice, and health policy has the potential to reduce disparities, promote earlier diagnosis, and improve gastric cancer outcomes in the United States.

43006908.title: US geographical disparities in young-onset colorectal cancer mortality, 1990-2023.
43006908.author: Wu JF
43006908.abstract: Among the 5 leading causes of cancer death in people younger than 50 years in the US, colorectal cancer (CRC) is the only one with increasing mortality. Using Global Burden of Disease 2023 estimates, we examined young-onset CRC mortality among persons aged 15-49 years from 1990 through 2023. Age-standardized mortality rates (ASMRs) and Joinpoint trends were calculated, with change summarized by the 2014-2023 mean annual percentage change (APC). In 2023, the ASMR was 3.25 per 100,000 and varied more than twofold across states; the mean APC was 1.06%. Ten of 13 states in the highest ASMR quartile were in the South, whereas the fastest increases were in the West. Five hotspot states had both highest-quartile ASMR and mean APC: Alaska, Kentucky, Missouri, New Mexico, and Tennessee. Overall, 65.5% of deaths were jointly attributable to assessed GBD risks; behavioral and metabolic PAFs were 56.1% and 21.6%, respectively.

43002724.title: Geographic Disparities in Oncology Access: A National Geospatial Analysis of Workforce Distribution and Fellowship Expansion.
43002724.author: Crowley RJ
43002724.abstract:
PURPOSE: Geographic disparities in access to oncology care in the United States persist because of the maldistribution of oncologists and training programs. The aim of this study was to identify optimal oncologist placements to maximize coverage, detect large clusters of unmet patient need, and evaluate factors associated with new oncology fellowship program establishment.
METHODS: We performed a national geospatial analysis from 2015 to 2025 using data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the National Resident Matching Program, and the US Census. A maximal coverage location problem (MCLP) model with a 40-km service radius identified optimal oncologist placements. Hierarchical density-based clustering found geographic clusters of unmet need. A Firth logistic regression model assessed county-level predictors of new fellowship program establishment.
RESULTS: Median baseline state-level oncologist coverage was highest in the Northeast and lowest in the Midwest and South. The MCLP model identified 5,578 additional oncologist placements that could extend coverage to 26.1 million patients aged 55 years and older; 52.2% of placements were in rural counties. Clustering revealed 910 areas of unmet need, including large underserved populations in Nevada, California, and Florida. Oncology fellowship programs increased from 140 to 180 between 2015 and 2025, with minimal rural growth (0.6%-1.7%). Higher income, greater oncologist density, and Medicaid expansion predicted new program establishment, while rurality was strongly negatively associated.
CONCLUSION: Significant geographic disparities in oncology access remain. Targeted workforce expansion, particularly in rural areas, could improve coverage; however, current fellowship growth patterns risk reinforcing existing inequities. Strategic, data-driven expansion of oncologists and training programs is needed to promote equitable cancer care access.

43034977.title: MRI-defined necrosis morphology, circulating immune profiles and survival in glioblastoma.
43034977.author: Gagliardi F
43034977.abstract:
PURPOSE: Necrosis is a defining feature and an active hypoxic niche implicated in immune escape and treatment resistance in glioblastoma (GBM). We asked whether MRI-defined necrosis morphology is associated with circulating immune profiles and overall survival (OS).
METHODS: We retrospectively studied 111 patients with newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype GBM resected in 2018-2024. Preoperative necrosis was classified visually as classic confluent or multiloculated. Two blinded readers reclassified all cases independently. Immune subsets were assessed by flow cytometry (n = 59, 48/11 classic/multiloculated) and plasma cytokines by multiplex immunoassay (n = 54, 45/9). All 28 immune analytes were exploratory, corrected across the panel. OS from surgery was analyzed with Kaplan-Meier and Cox models, including treatment and small-sample sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: Inter-reader agreement was kappa = 0.883. Multiloculated morphology was associated with longer OS (median, 17.4 vs. 14.4 months; HR, 0.55, 95% CI, 0.31-0.98, p = 0.041), including after multivariable adjustment (n = 94; HR, 0.42, 0.22-0.81, p = 0.010; Firth-penalized, 0.44, p = 0.007), exclusion of untreated patients and early deaths, and restriction to completed chemoradiation (HR, 0.37, 0.16-0.84, p = 0.018). Classic morphology was associated with fewer conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) (0.15% vs. 0.41%, p = 0.006), more mature natural killer cells (p = 0.022), and lower granzyme B, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, and IL-10, but no difference survived correction (lowest q = 0.088). Multiloculated patients were younger (57.2 vs. 64.3 years, p = 0.032). The cDC association did not persist after adjustment for deep-seated location (p = 0.124).
CONCLUSIONS: Multiloculated necrosis was associated with longer OS after adjustment for established prognostic factors, which requires external validation. Circulating immune differences were exploratory and could not be separated from tumor location.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

43033317.title: Long-term socioeconomic, psychiatric, and societal burden in patients with grade 2 mIDH glioma and partner spillover burden, worsening with disease progression and RT/CT initiation.
43033317.author: Skjøth-Rasmussen J
43033317.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Grade 2 mIDH gliomas affect adults of working age and may disrupt everyday functioning, work capacity, and family life for many years. We assessed long-term socioeconomic, healthcare, and psychiatric burden among patients initially managed with active observation and their partners.
METHODS: This Danish nationwide observational matched cohort study included patients with incident grade 2 mIDH diffuse astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma diagnosed from 2010 to 2022. Patients receiving radiotherapy (RT) and/or chemotherapy (CT), palliative care, or dying within six months after diagnosis were excluded. Patients and partners were compared with coarsened exact matched population controls and outcomes were followed up to 10 years post-index and stratified by RT/CT treatment exposure.
RESULTS: The study included 237 patients and 113 partners, matched to 1,161 patient controls and 550 partner controls. Ten-year overall patient survival was 72.7%. Patients experienced a profound and increasing burden: Over 10 years, they averaged - 163,000€ lost pay-check income and accumulated + 347,000€ combined incremental burden from public benefits, healthcare costs, and productivity loss (RT/CT-exposed: +513,000€, RT/CT unexposed: +163,000€) compared to controls. Partners maintained stable income and employment, but partners of RT/CT-exposed patients had increased work absence, averaging + 2.8 excess weeks annually (approximately twice the excess seen among partners of RT/CT-unexposed patients, + 1.4 weeks).
CONCLUSION: Grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma imposes a significant, progressive long term multidimensional burden on patients and society. Disease progression and RT/CT initiation marks a clinically meaningful trajectory shift towards profoundly worse outcomes for patients and partners.

43023458.title: Vorasidenib in IDH1/2-mutant low-grade gliomas: a prospective study on volumetric MRI and seizure outcome.
43023458.author: Rudà R
43023458.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The IDH1/2 inhibitor vorasidenib demonstrated efficacy in residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant gliomas after surgery. However, there is lack of knowledge regarding factors predicting the probability of response.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a prospective single-centre study on 54 grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant astrocytomas and IDH1/2-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas treated with vorasidenib. MRI response (2D and 3D) and seizure outcome were longitudinally assessed. Factors associated with response were explored using regression models.
RESULTS: With a median follow-up of 17.5 months, vorasidenib induced progressive tumour shrinkage on MRI, with median volume reductions of - 12.2% at cycle 6, -27.8% at cycle 12, and -55.5% at cycle 18. Best volumetric response was CR in 1 patient, PR in 5, MR in 9, SD in 31 and PD in 7. The ORR (CR + PR + MR) was 28%. Eighteen patients who had focal grade 3 areas showed similar volumetric response and ORR. 9/12 (75%) patients with baseline seizures achieved ≥50% reduction or seizure freedom. MRI response correlated with early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction. Vorasidenib was generally well tolerated, with liver enzyme elevation being the main adverse event.
CONCLUSIONS: Vorasidenib induced sustained tumour shrinkage and seizure control. Early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction were associated with MRI response.

43023427.title: B7-H3-targeted natural killer cells are effective against atypical teratoid / rhabdoid tumors and extend survival in orthotopic xenografts.
43023427.author: Choe J
43023427.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors (ATRTs) are the most common malignant CNS tumor in infants, and patients suffer from low survival rates and treatment-related morbidities. These tumors frequently overexpress the pan-cancer antigen B7-H3 (CD276), which can be targeted with immunotherapy. We hypothesized that adding a B7-H3-targeting cytotoxic chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) to NK cells can enhance killing against ATRTs.
METHODS: We designed a library of variable affinity B7-H3-targeted CARs, which were transduced into primary healthy donor-derived NK cells. We verified B7-H3 expression in a panel of ATRT cell lines and further engineered luciferase and nuclear GFP-expressing ATRT (CHLA-04, CHLA-06, BT12, BT37) as well as a CHLA-06-derived B7-H3 knockout. We tested CAR-NK cell functionality using in vitro co-culture cytotoxicity assays. We delivered anti-B7-H3 CAR-NK cells intratumorally or intracerebroventricularly (ICV) to ATRT orthotopic xenografts and monitored for tumor growth and animal survival.
RESULTS: B7-H3-targeted CAR-NK cells demonstrated target-specific cytotoxicity when compared to unmodified NK cells. Knockout of B7-H3 in target cells abolished the increased CAR-mediated target killing. When delivered intratumorally to CHLA-06 orthotopic xenograft-bearing mice, anti-B7-H3 CAR-NK cells eliminated tumor cells and prolonged survival. When CAR-NK cells were delivered ICV against a CNS disseminated tumor model of BT12, treated mice had significantly improved survival.
CONCLUSIONS: Anti-B7-H3 CAR-NK cells effectively kill ATRTs in multiple pre-clinical in vitro and in vivo models in an antigen-specific manner. Evidence of efficacy in translationally relevant models provides support for using B7-H3-targeting CAR-NK cells in high-risk ATRT patients.

43021670.title: Longitudinal evolution of O-(2-[18F]-fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine PET metrics in serial imaging during glioblastoma progression.
43021670.author: Galldiks N
43021670.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Most studies evaluating O-(2-[18F]-fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine (FET) PET for glioblastoma progression rely on single-scan assessments, leaving diagnostic uncertainties in cases with borderline tracer uptake. We evaluated metabolic activity evolution during the transition of glioblastoma progression using serial FET PET to determine whether longitudinal parameter changes improve diagnostic certainty.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Between 2016 and 2026, 182 patients with glioblastoma undergoing 690 dynamic FET PET scans (median, 3; range, 2-12) were retrospectively evaluated. Eligible cases required documented progressive disease according to RANO 2.0 criteria and serial FET PET at least 2 time points (at suspected progression and within a 6-month prior window). Static PET parameters, ie tumor-to-brain ratios (TBRmean, TBRmax) and metabolic tumor volume (MTV), and their longitudinal changes were evaluated according to PET RANO 1.0 criteria, alongside additional dynamic PET parameters (time-to-peak). Single-scan metrics and serial changes were compared in cases with borderline uptake.
RESULTS: Ninety patients with 102 confirmed progression events met all selection criteria (median interscan interval, 2.7 months). At progression, TBRmean, TBRmax, and MTV increased significantly (P < .001). Median percentage increases were modest for TBRmean (+4%) and TBRmax (+17%), whereas MTV exhibited a substantial expansion (+182%). In cases with borderline uptake, applying a longitudinal MTV increase criterion of ≥40% per PET RANO 1.0 substantially improved progression detection to up to 89%, yielding a 14% higher diagnostic detection rate compared to single-scan thresholds.
CONCLUSIONS: In glioblastomas with documented RANO 2.0 progression, integrating longitudinal MTV changes markedly improves diagnostic certainty over single-scan uptake metrics, particularly in challenging cases with borderline uptake.

43021570.title: MGMT Protein Expression and Promoter Methylation in Glioblastoma Survival: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
43021570.author: van Heumen M
43021570.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. Methylation of the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter is the only clinically used biomarker predicting response to alkylating agents such as temozolomide and is associated with improved survival. However, its predictive accuracy is limited by an intermediate gray zone and variability in assessment methods. To reduce overtreatment of patients, improved stratification strategies are needed, potentially through integration of additional biomarkers such as MGMT protein expression.
METHODS: We performed a systematic review to evaluate studies comparing the prognostic value for progression-free survival and overall survival of MGMT promoter methylation and MGMT protein expression in glioblastoma patients treated with temozolomide, including 33 independent cohorts with a total of 4,691 patients. We searched three databases up to May 2025. Risk of bias was assessed with a modified Quips tool.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Methylation-specific PCR and pyrosequencing indicated stronger prognostic value than immunohistochemical assessment of MGMT protein expression with hazard ratios (HRs) of 2.07 (95%CI 1.61-2.66), 2.13 (95%CI 1.64-2.75), and 1.50 (95%CI 1.26-1.79), respectively. An inverse correlation between MGMT promoter methylation and protein expression was observed in only 52% of assessed studies, suggesting that promoter methylation and protein expression may contribute independently to prognosis.
CONCLUSION: Substantial variability in methylation assays and protein cut-offs underscores the need for methodological harmonization in future studies and clinical practice. Integration of MGMT protein expression with promoter methylation refines identification of primary temozolomide-resistant tumors and supports the debate of withholding temozolomide in patients unlikely to benefit.

43018787.title: Diffusion anisotropy as an imaging biomarker of directional progression in temporal glioblastoma.
43018787.author: Fares J
43018787.abstract:
PURPOSE: Glioblastoma frequently progresses beyond surgical margins, yet whether preoperative imaging can predict its direction remains unclear. Given the anatomical characteristics of the temporal lobe and the potential role of anterior temporal lobectomy, we evaluated FLAIR, isotropic diffusion (DTI-p), and diffusion anisotropy (DTI-q) as imaging biomarkers of directional progression after complete resection.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed a prospectively recruited multicenter cohort of patients with newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype glioblastoma confined to the temporal lobe who underwent complete resection of contrast-enhancing tumor and had preoperative diffusion tensor imaging and follow-up MRI demonstrating progression. Progression was visually classified relative to the resection cavity. Direction-specific accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were calculated, with paired comparisons using exact McNemar tests and Holm correction across all comparisons. Times to progression and death were summarized descriptively.
RESULTS: Thirty-two patients met inclusion criteria. DTI-q demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy across all progression directions (median, 75%), compared with DTI-p (median, 50%) and FLAIR (median, 44%). DTI-q significantly outperformed FLAIR and DTI-p for lateral, superior, and inferior progression after Holm correction. Combined imaging models did not improve predictive performance over DTI-q alone.
CONCLUSION: Preoperative DTI-q predicted directional progression after complete resection more accurately than FLAIR or DTI-p, supporting DTI-q as a potential imaging biomarker for spatially informed surgical planning.

43016311.title: AI Assessment of Heterogeneous Histopathologic Brain Tumor Sub-regions: the RANO MICCAI BraTS-Path 2024 Challenge.
43016311.author: Thakur SP
43016311.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Automated classification of glioblastoma (IDH-wt, WHO CNS Gr.4) histopathologic sub-regions in whole slide images (WSI) is essential for quantitative tumor characterization, but faces substantial challenges from intra-tumoral heterogeneity and inter-observer annotation variability. The AI-RANO & RANO-Pathology working groups organized BraTS-Path 2024, representing the first international benchmarking environment and publicly available spatially annotated dataset, towards promoting the development and fair evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to classify specific sub-regions: cellular tumor, pseudopalisading necrosis (PN), microvascular proliferation, geographic necrosis, infiltration into the cortex, and white matter penetration (WM).
METHODS: Multi-institutional H&E-stained WSIs had reference standard samples generated by eight expert neuropathologists, following a rigorous peer review protocol, resulting in 309,118 data samples (training/validation/hold-out testing: 96,485/62,387/150,246). Quantitative performance evaluation of six AI approaches was conducted based on multiple metrics, including Accuracy and Matthew's correlation coefficient (MCC). A robust statistically-aware ranking strategy offered statistical significance of the final rankings.
RESULTS: Top-performing approaches employed common strategies, including large pre-trained models, ensembling, and extensive data augmentation, reporting Accuracy=0.69 and MCC=0.58. Key challenges included severe class imbalance, hampering minority class performance, and inter-annotator variability, especially for ambiguous sub-regions such as PN or WM.
CONCLUSIONS: BraTS-Path represents a valuable public resource for glioblastoma histopathologic sub-region assessment. Our findings indicate the specific task remaining an open research problem, highlighting the influence of rare sub-regions, the absence of a consistent "gold standard" annotation protocol, and the potential of foundation models to improve generalization, guiding future research toward developing more reliable AI tools for quantitative neuropathology.

43013158.title: Clinically-relevant pathological discordance in multicentric IDH-mutant gliomas: a single institution case series.
43013158.author: Lai TJ
43013158.abstract:
PURPOSE: Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutations are truncal driver events in low-grade gliomas. While multifocal gliomas are presumed to spread metastatically and share identical pathology, the biological nature of IDH mutant multicentric gliomas remains poorly understood.
METHODS: We retrospectively identified patients with radiographically distinct multicentric gliomas where ≥ 1 lesion was IDH-mutant. We analyzed the subset with multi​focal tissue sampling using available histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and next-generation sequencing across distinct foci to render updated CNS WHO diagnoses based on integrated molecular data.
RESULTS: Of 46 multicentric IDH-mutant gliomas, eight patients (17%) underwent multifocal sampling. Of six synchronous cases, three exhibited mismatched foundational drivers, one showed divergent clonal evolution (discordant 1p/19q codeletion), and two demonstrated asynchronous malignant progression. Differing pathology between the lesions directly influenced clinical decision-making in three of the synchronous cases. The remaining two cases presented metachronously. Structured review of surgical decision-making in 35 evaluable patients without multifocal sampling revealed that in 71% (25/35) of reviewed cases, tissue sampling of the additional lesion was not pursued for lesion-level (poor stereotactic target, diagnostic uncertainty) or patient-level reasons. In the remaining 29% (10/35), the additional lesion was determined to be amenable to biopsy or resection, yet sampling was deferred on the presumption of pathological concordance with the index lesion.
CONCLUSION: Multicentric IDH-mutant gliomas exhibit significant spatial and temporal heterogeneity driven by diverse oncogenic and clonal evolution. Because radiographic congruence does not guarantee histo-molecular congruence, multi​focal tissue acquisition with detailed morphologic and genetic profiling should become the standard clinical approach whenever feasible to prevent diagnostic misclassification and optimize individualized therapy.

43013157.title: Center-dependent "non-operability" in diffuse glioma: challenging assumptions through awake resection.
43013157.author: Elia A
43013157.abstract:
PURPOSE: The concept of non-operability in diffuse glioma remains poorly standardized and may reflect institutional experience rather than absolute surgical limitations. We evaluated whether patients previously deemed "non-operable" by outside institutions could undergo awake craniotomy and achieve outcomes comparable to those of patients initially considered operable.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 448 adults who underwent awake function-based craniotomy for a diffuse glioma (2011-2024). Sixty-six patients (14.7%) had previously been considered "non-operable" and were compared with patients initially considered operable. Feasibility, safety, and were assessed using propensity score matching and voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping.
RESULTS: Patients in the "non operable group" more frequently had prior oncological treatments, focal neurological deficits, larger tumor volumes, greater midline mass effect, and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Despite greater preoperative complexity, feasibility, safety, and efficacy outcomes did not significantly differ between groups, including intraoperative adverse events, surgery-related complications, 6-month postoperative Karnofsky Performance Status score and seizure control, extent of resection, and residual tumor volume. No awake procedure was aborted in the "non-operable" group. Propensity score-matched confirmed these findings. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identified no independent anatomical predictor of prior non-operability designation.
CONCLUSION: In selected patients referred for a second opinion, a prior "non-operable" designation did not preclude safe awake resection, suggesting that non-operability may partly reflect a center-related judgment. Patients initially deemed "non-operable" can achieve outcomes comparable to those of conventionally considered operable patients when managed in specialized high-volume centers with expertise in awake function-based craniotomy. These findings support systematic consideration of referral for a second opinion in such patients.

43012930.title: Carmustine-releasing wafers for brain metastasis: single institution experience and results of the VIGILANT registry.
43012930.author: Smith EC
43012930.abstract:
PURPOSE: Brain metastases affect many patients with solid tumor malignancies. Treatments include surgery, radiation, immunotherapy, and CNS-penetrating chemotherapy. Nonetheless, rates of CNS-related tumor death remain high. Local recurrence after radiosurgery and lesions with a V12 too high for radiosurgery present a particular challenge. The VIGILANT (Vigilant Observation of GLIADEL Wafer Implant) registry prospectively examined use and efficacy of carmustine-releasing wafers which includes patients with brain metastases [1]. Here we present a retrospective analysis of patients with brain metastasis from the VIGILANT registry.
METHODS: Forty-seven patients were observed after surgical resection of brain metastasis and GLIADEL implantation at Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center. Thirty-eight patients underwent treatment for local recurrence following radiosurgery. Nine had lesions treated that were deemed too large for successful primary radiosurgery. Patients were evaluated primarily for overall survival (OS) and progression free survival (PFS) from the date of surgery, and secondarily for adverse events and local progression.
RESULTS: Median OS was 23 months. Of 25 deaths, 7 (28%) met criteria for CNS-tumor related etiology. 24 (51.1%) patients had progression during follow up, 6 (12.8%) had local progression. 2 (4.3%) overall had local progression that required additional neurosurgical treatment. Of 9 patients not previously treated with radiosurgery, 4 (44.4%) had no progression. Of 5 patients who received GLIADEL as their upfront cranial intervention, none had local recurrence. 43 patients had adverse events; 2 considered possibly GLIADEL related.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-institution retrospective analysis of prospectively collected registry data, patients undergoing resection and carmustine wafer implantation after prior radiosurgery or for lesions considered unsuitable for primary radiosurgery had favorable observed survival (OS 23 months), intracranial progression (1-year local progression rate of 12%), and minimal related adverse-event outcomes.

43012912.title: Does timing matter? Early postoperative Gamma Knife radiosurgery within 14 days is associated with longer overall survival after brain metastasis resection.
43012912.author: Sinha S
43012912.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The optimal timing of postoperative Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) following brain metastasis resection remains uncertain. We evaluated the association between surgery-to-GKRS timing and overall survival (OS) and local recurrence-free survival (LRFS).
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 182 patients who underwent initial postoperative cavity-directed GKRS following brain metastasis resection between May 2007 through February 2025. Surgery-to-GKRS timing was evaluated continuously and using outcome-oriented cutpoint analysis across intervals of 7-60 days. Survival outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression, with additional sensitivity analyses evaluating cutpoint stability and potential confounding.
RESULTS: The median surgery-to-GKRS interval was 19.5 days. Treatment within 14 days demonstrated the greatest observed OS separation, with median survival of 37.8 versus 15.3 months for patients treated later (log-rank p = 0.0123). This association persisted after multivariable adjustment (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.38-1.00; p = 0.0491) and additional adjustment for calendar year of surgery (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37-0.97; p = 0.037). However, the 14-day threshold did not retain statistical significance after adjustment for outcome-oriented cutpoint selection (p = 0.181). GKRS timing was not significantly associated with LRFS.
CONCLUSIONS: GKRS within 14 days of brain metastasis resection was associated with substantially longer overall survival, highlighting the potential clinical importance of timely postoperative radiosurgical care. Although the optimal treatment interval remains uncertain, these findings support early referral, efficient multidisciplinary coordination, and minimizing avoidable treatment delays.

43009619.title: Serial serum lactate dehydrogenase dynamics as an adjunctive biomarker for differentiating true progression from treatment-related changes in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma.
43009619.author: Donnini F
43009619.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Differentiating true tumor progression from pseudoprogression and radiation necrosis remains a major clinical challenge in patients with IDH-wild-type glioblastoma after radiotherapy and temozolomide. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is inexpensive, widely available and repeatable, but it is a nonspecific systemic marker whose tissue source cannot be inferred from total serum activity. We therefore evaluated serial LDH dynamics as an adjunctive, hypothesis-generating biomarker rather than as a glioblastoma-specific tumor marker.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients treated at a single tertiary neuro-oncology center with histologically confirmed IDH-wild-type glioblastoma who developed new or increasing contrast enhancement after standard radiochemotherapy and had available serum LDH measurements at baseline and at the time of suspicious MRI. Final diagnosis was assigned using histology when available or a composite reference standard based on multidisciplinary review and longitudinal imaging follow-up. LDH at suspicious MRI and LDH percentage change from baseline were evaluated for their ability to distinguish true progression from treatment-related changes.
RESULTS: The cohort included 180 patients: 101 with true progression and 79 with treatment-related changes, including 65 pseudoprogression and 14 radiation necrosis cases. Median LDH at suspicious MRI was higher in true progression than in treatment-related changes (371 vs 273 U/L), as was median LDH percentage increase from baseline (28.7% vs 5.8%). Baseline LDH showed limited discrimination (AUC 0.675), whereas event LDH and LDH percentage change showed stronger performance (AUC 0.855 and 0.872, respectively). An exploratory LDH signature, defined as event LDH ≥ 293 U/L or LDH increase ≥ 25%, showed high sensitivity (95.0%) and negative predictive value (90.0%) but moderate specificity (57.0%).
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center retrospective cohort, serial total-serum LDH dynamics were associated with final diagnostic classification after suspicious post-treatment MRI in IDH-wild-type glioblastoma. Because serum LDH is biologically nonspecific and the present study did not determine LDH isoenzymes or cellular origin, LDH should not be interpreted as a glioma-specific tumor marker or used as a stand-alone test. Its potential role is limited to an adjunctive signal within a multimodal RANO-informed diagnostic framework, and prospective external validation with source-resolved LDH analyses is required.

43007519.title: Chromosome 14q loss is associated with adverse survival and a distinct transcriptional phenotype in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.
43007519.author: Higa N
43007519.abstract:
PURPOSE: In IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, prognostic biomarkers beyond MGMT promoter methylation remain limited. Chromosome 14q contains candidate tumor suppressors, yet the significance of arm-level 14q loss in molecularly defined glioblastoma is unclear.
METHODS: Arm-level 14q status was inferred from coordinated 14q expression (Gaussian-mixture model) in bulk RNA sequencing of 215 Japanese IDH-wildtype glioblastomas and validated against methylation-array copy number (n = 42). Associations with outcome and transcriptional programs were evaluated and assessed in CGGA (n = 74) and TCGA (n = 139) using the discovery-cohort threshold.
RESULTS: RNA-seq-based calls agreed with array copy number in 40/42 cases (κ = 0.90). 14q loss (87/215, 40.5%) was associated with shorter overall (p = 0.0053) and progression-free survival (p = 0.0175), remaining prognostic in the prespecified multivariable model (hazard ratio 1.44, 95% confidence interval 1.02-2.01; p = 0.036). 14q loss and MGMT promoter hypomethylation were prognostically complementary (four-group p < 0.0001). Chromosome 14-excluded, purity-adjusted gene set enrichment analysis showed increased E2F-target and G2M-checkpoint and reduced oxidative-phosphorylation and lipid-metabolism programs in 14q-loss tumors. The survival association was reproduced in CGGA (p = 0.0012) but not in TCGA (p = 0.55), with significant heterogeneity (interaction p = 0.005).
CONCLUSION: RNA-seq-inferable 14q loss identifies a clinically adverse subgroup of Japanese IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, is complementary to MGMT promoter methylation, and is associated with a proliferation-high, oxidative-phosphorylation-low transcriptional state. The absence of this association in TCGA underscores the need for validation in additional population-diverse cohorts before clinical implementation.

43007513.title: Explainable machine learning predictive models for treatment response after SBRT in melanoma brain metastases.
43007513.author: Cilla S
43007513.abstract:
PURPOSE/OBJECTIVE: To develop an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model to predict the complete/partial response of oligometastatic brain lesions from melanoma (MBMs) two months after from radiosurgical or fractionated stereotactic treatments.
MATERIAL/METHODS: 50 consecutive patients with a total 102 MBMs treated with CyberKnife® SBRT from December 2012 to December 2018 were selected within the Rabbit study. Local response was evaluated on brain MRI performed during follow-up using response evaluation criteria in solid tumors (RECIST) and revised using response criteria for brain metastases from the response assessment in neuro-oncology criteria (RANO) group. For each treated lesion, the following variables were considered: number of treated lesions, the LDH pre-treatment level, previous treatments (surgery or whole brain RT), BRAF status, time from primary diagnosis to brain lesions discovery (Time_diag), lesion dimensions and site, SBRT dose and fractionation, type of concomitant treatment with ipilimumab (IPI). Six different supervised machine learning models, including logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), decision tree (DT) and light gradient boosting (LGBM), were trained and internally validated with 5-fold cross validation. Model performances were assessed using receiving operator curves (ROC) and area under the curve (AUC). An explainable approach based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method was deployed to generate individual explanations of the model decisions. Lastly, a decision tree was created to better understand and interpret the complex relationships between the covariates and the target variable.
RESULTS: 23.5% of lesions had a complete or partial response and were used as ground truth for the ML models. The best performing model was the LGBM, reporting a mean AUCs in the 5-fold cross validation of 0.87 (0.85-0.91). SHAP analysis strongly associated complete/partial response with four variables, namely in order of importance: the BRAF status, the total dose, the type of treatment with ipilimumab, and the lesion dimension. In particular, the DT classified patients with BRAF "wild-type" status having only 10.7% probability to reach complete/partial response. Among these lesions, those treated with doses < 24 Gy had 0% probability of complete/partial response. By contrast, lesions with a BRAF "mutated" status reported a probability of complete/partial response of 39.1%. Among these lesions, those treated with concomitant ipilimumab reached 100% probability of complete/partial response.
CONCLUSION: Machine-learning models enable a reliable prediction of the treatment response of oligometastatic lesions receiving SBRT. This approach may assist radiation oncologists to tailor more individualized treatment plans in this clinical setting. An external validation of the results is mandatory.

43006914.title: Molecular profiling uncovers KCa2.3 as key driver of pacemaker cells in glioblastoma.
43006914.author: Hoffmann DC
43006914.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Glioblastoma is orchestrated by pacemaker cancer cells, a rare population preferentially residing at the hubs of tumor cell networks. These cells autonomously generate periodic Ca2+ oscillations that drive glioblastoma network function, resilience, and disease progression. To date, the Ca2+-activated K+ channel KCa3.1 is the only known driver of pacemaker function, calling for studies to identify additional factors - to better understand a key component of glioblastoma pathobiology, and uncover novel therapeutic targets.
METHODS: A molecular Ca2+ integrator technology enabled the transcriptional profiling of highly Ca2+-active glioblastoma cells, a population enriched for pacemaker cells. Putative regulators of pacemaker function were interrogated using genetic, pharmacological, and computational approaches across complementary glioblastoma models.
RESULTS: We identified a distinct transcriptional program that captures highly Ca2+ active glioblastoma cells, including pacemaker cells, across preclinical models and human glioblastoma specimens. This program comprised upregulated cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes, TM-network markers (Aquaporin-4 and Cystatin C), and the Ca2+-activated K+ channels KCa1.1 and KCa2.3. Amongst these components, in silico modeling identified KCa2.3 as the only channel compatible with executing pacemaker function. Consistently, KCa2.3 expression was increased in pacemaker cells, and both genetic and pharmacological perturbation of KCa2.3 selectively disrupted pacemaker function, resulting in reduced network-wide Ca2+ activity. Ultimately, pharmacological inhibition of KCa2.3 with edelfosine reduced tumor burden in human brain spheroids.
CONCLUSIONS: We present the first experimental approach to characterize molecular factors of glioblastoma pacemaker cells in a broad and unbiased manner, and identify KCa2.3 as a novel pacemaker gene and promising therapeutic target.

43004079.title: Epilepsy in women with progestogen-associated intracranial meningiomas.
43004079.author: Hudelist B
43004079.abstract:
PURPOSE: Progestogen-associated intracranial meningiomas are increasingly recognized as a distinct clinical entity, often characterized by multiplicity and preferential skull-base location. However, epilepsy in this population remains poorly characterized. We aimed to assess the prevalence, clinical features, and factors associated with epilepsy in women with progestogen-associated meningiomas.
METHOD: We retrospectively analyzed consecutive adult women managed for intracranial meningioma at a tertiary neuro-oncology center between 2000 and 2024, with documented exposure to at least one progestogen associated with increased meningioma risk and available clinical and imaging data. Epilepsy was analyzed at the patient level using one index meningioma per patient. Given the low number of epilepsy events, analyses were descriptive.
RESULTS: A total of 209 women were included (mean age 51.9 ± 10.1 years), including 69 (33.0%) with multiple meningiomas. Epilepsy at diagnosis occurred in 4.8% of patients and in 13.3% of symptomatic patients. Patients with epilepsy had larger index meningiomas than those without (24.6±24.3 vs 8.8 ± 16.9 cm3), more frequent meningioma-related brain edema (70.0% vs 19.1%), and more frequent midline mass effect (60.0% vs 13.6%). No association was detected with progestogen type or exposure pattern. Following antiseizure medication initiation, seizures were controlled in all patients with epilepsy at diagnosis. At last follow-up, seizures were controlled in 7/9 (77.8%) evaluable patients. During follow-up, de novo epilepsy remained uncommon, particularly among patients initially managed conservatively.
CONCLUSION: Epilepsy is uncommon in women with progestogen-associated intracranial meningiomas. When present, it appears to be primarily related to tumor burden and meningioma-brain interface involvement, whereas no association with specific progestogen exposure characteristics was detected.

43002189.title: Pre-operative stereotactic radiosurgery versus intraoperative cesium-131 brachytherapy for resected brain metastases: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
43002189.author: Kite T
43002189.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pre-operative stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and intraoperative cesium-131 (Cs-131) brachytherapy are alternatives to post-operative SRS for resected brain metastases (BMs). The randomized phase 3 Radiation One and Done Study (ROADS; NCT04365374) showed improved surgical-bed control with Cs-131 tiles versus post-operative stereotactic radiotherapy, but outcomes relative to pre-operative SRS are undefined.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and ScienceDirect were searched through October 2026 (PRISMA 2020); one further trial was identified by other methods. Twelve-month local control (LC), leptomeningeal disease (LMD), radiation necrosis (RN), and overall survival (OS) were extracted for treatment-naïve BMs. Proportions were pooled with random-effects generalized linear mixed models and compared with a test for subgroup differences; sensitivity analyses included meta-regression, Hartung-Knapp, leave-one-out, follow-up, and fractionation analyses.
RESULTS: Fifteen pre-operative SRS studies (918 patients/940 BMs) and four brachytherapy studies (207 patients/217 BMs) were included. Pooled 12-month LC was 97% (95% CI 90-99) with Cs-131 brachytherapy and 90% (86-93) with pre-operative SRS (test for subgroup differences p = 0.054; meta-regression p = 0.019; Hartung-Knapp p = 0.066); among studies reporting observed counts, LC was 99% vs. 90% (p = 0.009). Within pre-operative SRS, LC was 96% after hypofractionated and 86% after single-fraction treatment (p = 0.005). LMD (9.1% vs. 5.1%) and RN (0.7% vs. 5.2%) did not differ significantly. Median OS was 15.6 months with brachytherapy (range 5.9-42.5; 11.0 months, range 5.9-20.1, excluding the ROADS estimate) and 14.4 months with pre-operative SRS (range 6.3-26.4).
CONCLUSION: Both approaches achieved high LC with low rates of LMD and RN. There was a trend towards higher LC with Cs-131 brachytherapy than with pre-operative SRS (97% vs. 90%; p = 0.054), and significantly so among studies reporting observed counts (99% vs. 90%; p = 0.009). Hypofractionated pre-operative SRS achieved LC similar to that of brachytherapy, suggesting that the difference may reflect single-fraction dose de-escalation rather than an intrinsic advantage of either modality. The two techniques may serve complementary roles, and prospective comparative study is warranted.
REGISTRATION: This review was not registered in PROSPERO.

43031331.title: TROP-2-Directed ADC Could Be New Standard for Some NSCLCs.
43031331.abstract: In the phase III Opti-TROP-Lung06 trial, patients with newly diagnosed PD-L1-negative, advanced nonsquamous non-small cell lung cancer without targetable alterations who received the TROP-2-directed antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab tirumotecan and the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab experienced a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 15 months. In comparison, those patients who received standard chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab experienced a median PFS of 5.7 months.

43025593.title: Circulating tumor DNA to direct adjuvant immunotherapy across mismatch repair-deficient solid tumors.
43025593.author: Janjigian YY
43025593.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Detection of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) harboring mutations that match those identified in resected tumor tissue signals occult residual disease after curative-intent surgery. Such patients are considered minimal residual disease (MRD)-positive and at high risk for recurrence and death. Few studies have shown that therapeutic intervention can alter recurrence risk in MRD-positive patients. We evaluated whether PD-1 blockade could reduce recurrence in MRD-positive patients with mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) tumors after curative-intent resection regardless of tumor site of origin.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: We initiated a prospective phase II interventional study in patients who had undergone curative-intent resection of early-stage dMMR tumors from any anatomic site. Postoperative MRD status was assessed by first identifying those patients who had detectable ctDNA and then confirming the ctDNA relevance to MRD by matching mutations detected in ctDNA to somatic mutations detected in resected tumor tissue. Confirmed MRD-positive patients received 6 months of PD-1 blockade and were evaluated for ctDNA clearance and 24-month recurrence-free survival (RFS). MRD-negative patients underwent observation.
RESULTS: We screened 184 patients with early-stage dMMR solid tumors after curative resection and tumor sequencing with ctDNA testing for MRD assessment. Twenty-three patients (12.5%) were MRD-positive; after excluding one assigned to placebo and three with synchronous radiographic disease, 19 were eligible. Six developed recurrences before pembrolizumab initiation despite being disease-free at enrollment. The remaining 13 MRD-positive patients received 6 months of PD-1 blockade. ctDNA clearance at 6 months was achieved in 11 of 13 patients (85%). Five treated patients (38%) developed recurrence during follow-up. Median follow-up for the MRD-positive patients was 59 months (95% CI: 52-NR). Among 152 MRD-negative patients managed with observation, 14 (9%) developed recurrence during follow-up; 2-year RFS was 92%.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide evidence that ctDNA-guided adjuvant therapy may offer clinical benefit in dMMR tumors regardless of tissue of origin.

43025423.title: Antibiotics counteracting tumor-promoting dysbiosis in colorectal cancer.
43025423.author: Zitvogel L
43025423.abstract: Antibiotics usually sabotage immune checkpoint blockade. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Jiang et al. report that pulsed, anaerobe-directed metronidazole added to an anti-PD-1 antibody and a VEGF receptor inhibitor achieved encouraging progression-free survival in Fusobacterium nucleatum-positive microsatellite-stable metastatic colorectal cancer, selectively dismantling a pathobiont network without inducing global dysbiosis.

43025422.title: Targeting F.nucleatum with metronidazole plus tislelizumab and fruquintinib in MSS colorectal cancer: A multicenter phase 2 study.
43025422.author: Jiang S
43025422.abstract: Fusobacterium nucleatum has been linked to chemoresistance and immune evasion in colorectal cancer (CRC), but therapeutic strategies targeting this bacterium remain limited. In this multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 trial (NCT06356597), 33 patients with Fusobacterium nucleatum-positive, microsatellite-stable metastatic CRC received the combination treatment of tislelizumab, fruquintinib, and the antimicrobial metronidazole. The primary endpoint was met, with a median progression-free survival of 6.0 months. The objective response rate and disease control rate were 19.4% and 83.9%, respectively. Grade 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 30.3% of patients, with no grade 4 or 5 events. Metagenomic analysis showed that metronidazole reduced Fusobacterium nucleatum abundance. Exploratory analyses associated clinical benefit with enrichment of Lactobacillus species and nonresponse with Enterococcus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders sensitized germ-free mice to the treatment, which enhanced cytotoxic CD8+ T cell differentiation and reduced terminal exhaustion. These findings support further evaluation of this combination in Fusobacterium nucleatum-positive metastatic CRC.

43024836.title: Early Treatment Failure in Patients With Relapsed/Refractory Multiple Myeloma Receiving Bispecific T-Cell Engagers: Development and Validation of the CHARGE Prognostic Index.
43024836.author: Zanwar S
43024836.abstract:
PURPOSE: Outcomes with bispecific T-cell engagers (TCEs) in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) are heterogeneous. A practical tool to guide prognosis is needed. We developed a model integrating clinical, biological, and treatment-related variables to predict progression-free survival (PFS) in patients receiving B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)- or G-protein-coupled receptor class 5 member D-directed TCEs.
METHODS: We evaluated outcomes of 577 BCMA-directed and 366 talquetamab treatments across 15 US Multiple Myeloma Immunotherapy Consortium centers. Variables significantly associated with inferior PFS in a multivariate Cox model were incorporated into a prognostic score and validated in an independent multicenter International Myeloma Foundation cohort.
RESULTS: With a median follow-up of 8.4 months, the median PFS was 6.4 months (7.0 months for BCMA TCE; 6.1 months for talquetamab); 92% of patients were triple-class-refractory. Six variables significantly associated with inferior PFS-high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities (HRCAs) [del(17p) or ≥2 HRCAs], hyperferritinemia (≥600 ng/mL), anemia (hemoglobin <9 g/dL), early relapse (<18 months from frontline therapy), general performance status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status ≥2), and exposure to prior BCMA-directed therapy-were combined to form the CHARGE index, stratifying patients into three risk groups. The median PFS was 21.8 months (95% CI, 11.7 to not reached), 7.1 months (95% CI, 6.1 to 10.1), and 1.6 months (95% CI, 1.2 to 2.5) in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, respectively; hazard ratios (HRs) were 2.0 (95% CI, 1.5 to 2.7) and 4.8 (95% CI, 3.5 to 6.7) for intermediate- and high-risk versus low-risk groups. External validation (n = 173) showed that the median PFS was not reached, 7.0 months, and 3.0 months, with corresponding HRs of 2.9 (95% CI, 1.7 to 4.9) and 4.8 (95% CI, 2.6 to 8.7).
CONCLUSION: The CHARGE index provides a simplified and externally validated framework for predicting treatment outcomes in patients with RRMM receiving TCEs.

43024257.author: Anderer S

43018949.title: Izalontamab Brengitecan in Recurrent or Metastatic Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: The PANKU-Esophagus01 Randomized Clinical Trial.
43018949.author: Lu Z
43018949.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Effective therapy remains lacking for patients with advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) whose disease progressed after standard treatment. Izalontamab brengitecan, an epidermal growth factor receptor and human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate with a topoisomerase I inhibitor, Ed-04, has shown clinical activity in ESCC in a phase 1b study.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of izalontamab brengitecan compared with chemotherapy in patients with advanced ESCC who progressed after first-line programmed cell death 1 protein (PD-1)/programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase 3, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted across 80 hospitals in China. Patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC that had progressed with first-line PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy were enrolled. Between March 19, 2024, and August 1, 2025 (final follow-up, October 17, 2025), a total of 704 patients were screened, and 497 were enrolled and randomized.
INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either izalontamab brengitecan (n = 249; 2.5 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 every 3 weeks) or physician-selected chemotherapy (n = 248; irinotecan, paclitaxel, or docetaxel) every 3 weeks.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The dual primary end points were progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by blinded independent central review according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 and overall survival (OS).
RESULTS: Of 497 patients who underwent randomization (median age, 61.0 years [range, 34-76]; 448 male patients [90.1%]), 493 received study treatment. At this interim analysis, izalontamab brengitecan demonstrated statistically significant improvement in both PFS and OS. Median PFS by blinded independent central review was 4.17 months (95% CI, 3.61-4.53 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 1.97 months (95% CI, 1.61-2.73 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.40-0.63; log-rank P < .001). Median OS was 9.79 months (95% CI, 7.89-11.01 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 7.20 months (95% CI, 6.18-7.82 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.48-0.82; log-rank P < .001). Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 212 of 249 patients (85.1%) with izalontamab brengitecan and 147 of 248 patients (59.3%) with chemotherapy and were predominantly hematologic.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Izalontamab brengitecan significantly improved PFS and OS vs chemotherapy in patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC whose disease had progressed after first-line treatment. These findings support izalontamab brengitecan as a new second-line treatment for this population in China.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06304974.

43013837.title: Intismeran Autogene plus Pembrolizumab for Resected Stage IIB to IV Melanoma.
43013837.author: Long GV
43013837.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intismeran autogene (intismeran) is an individualized neoantigen therapy that is designed to induce new T-cell responses and expand preexisting T-cell responses against patient-specific tumor neoantigens, which may potentially improve the efficacy of adjuvant therapy in patients with melanoma.
METHODS: In this phase 3, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned patients with completely resected stage IIB to IV cutaneous melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive intramuscular intismeran (at a dose of 1 mg) or placebo every 3 weeks for nine doses; all the patients received intravenous pembrolizumab (at a dose of 400 mg) every 6 weeks for nine cycles. The primary end point was investigator-determined recurrence-free survival, assessed in a time-to-event analysis. Key secondary end points included investigator-determined distant-metastasis-free survival (assessed in a time-to-event analysis) and safety.
RESULTS: A total of 1137 patients underwent randomization: 757 to the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 380 to the placebo-pembrolizumab group. The median follow-up was 24.6 months. Recurrence-free survival at 24 months was 82.2% in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 70.0% in the placebo-pembrolizumab group (two-sided P<0.001); the piecewise hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.49) before 6 months and 0.42 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.58) after 6 months. Distant-metastasis-free survival at 24 months was 88.5% with intismeran-pembrolizumab and 80.2% with placebo-pembrolizumab (two-sided P = 0.002); the piecewise hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% CI, 0.58 to 1.79) before 6 months and 0.50 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.73) after 6 months. Adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 23.6% of the patients in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 20.3% of the patients in the placebo-pembrolizumab group. Eight patients (1.1%) in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group died from an adverse event; five of the deaths occurred before intismeran was administered.
CONCLUSIONS: Adjuvant therapy with intismeran plus pembrolizumab significantly prolonged recurrence-free survival and distant-metastasis-free survival as compared with pembrolizumab alone in patients with completely resected, high-risk cutaneous melanoma. (Funded by Merck Sharp and Dohme and Moderna; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05933577.).

43012674.title: Latent Squamous Plasticity Licensed by Chromatin-State Remodeling Dictates Therapeutic Susceptibility in Cholangiocarcinoma.
43012674.author: Yang C
43012674.abstract: Adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC) in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) has long been considered rare (~1-2%), yet its occurrence portends lethal disease progression. Here, we identify latent squamous plasticity, a transcriptionally primed yet histology-silent state that is quantifiable by a squamous transition potential (STP) index. Approximately 20-30% of iCCA patients can be classified as STP-high and experience ASC-like dismal outcomes. Mechanistically, FOSL1 acts as a plasticity trigger, driving a temporally ordered squamous program by reshaping the chromatin landscape. Additionally, it cooperates with p63 in an enhancer-dependent manner to dysregulate PTGS2/COX-2 expression. The resulting intratumoral PGE2 accumulation drives neutrophil-mediated FOXP3-negative type 1 regulatory T-cell (Tr1) polarization and predisposes STP-high tumors to immunotherapy resistance. Through a drug-repurposing screen, we identify celecoxib as a dual-function agent that counteracts latent squamous plasticity while fostering an immune-permissive state, providing a clinically actionable strategy for squamous-biased iCCA now being evaluated in a phase Ib/II trial (NCT07632235).

43008245.title: Treatment of Recurrent and/or Metastatic Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: CSCO and ASCO Joint Guideline.
43008245.author: Jiang W
43008245.abstract:
PURPOSE: To provide evidence-based recommendations on first- and subsequent-line systemic therapy, maintenance therapy, locoregional consolidation, and salvage local therapy for patients with recurrent and/or metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC).
METHODS: A multidisciplinary Expert Panel convened by CSCO and ASCO reviewed evidence from randomized trials, meta-analyses, systematic reviews, prospective and retrospective studies, and clinical experience. The guideline was informed by a systematic literature review and consensus-based interpretation of efficacy, safety, feasibility, and patient-centered outcomes across scenarios. Outcomes included overall and progression-free survival, response and disease control rates, toxicity, and quality of life.
RESULTS: Evidence supports platinum-based chemotherapy plus a programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitor as preferred first-line therapy for medically fit patients. Evidence also supports maintenance strategies after disease control, while treatment selection depends on prior treatment, disease extent, patient fitness, resource availability, and preferences. Selected responders may receive locoregional consolidation radiotherapy or oral maintenance chemotherapy. For isolated locoregional recurrence amenable to local therapy, options include salvage surgery and re-irradiation.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Chemotherapy plus a PD-1 inhibitor, followed by maintenance PD-1 inhibition for up to 2 years, should be offered first-line to appropriate patients with recurrent and/or metastatic NPC. Chemotherapy alone may be offered when immunotherapy is unsuitable or declined. Selected patients responding to first-line chemotherapy may receive oral maintenance chemotherapy or locoregional consolidation intensity-modulated radiotherapy. Salvage surgery or re-irradiation is recommended for appropriately selected patients with isolated locoregional recurrence. Subsequent-line options include chemotherapy, PD-1 inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates. Treatment should be individualized according to disease setting, prior therapy, expected toxicities, availability, local drug approvals, and patient preferences. Early supportive and specialist interdisciplinary palliative care, where available, should accompany active anticancer treatment for advanced, incurable disease.Additional information is available at www.ascopubs.org/topics/asco-guidelines/head-neck-cancer.

43008242.title: Treatment of Stage IB to III Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: CSCO-ASCO Guideline Update.
43008242.author: Chen YP
43008242.abstract:
PURPOSE: To update the 2021 CSCO-ASCO guideline on chemotherapy in combination with radiotherapy for the definitive treatment of non-metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), incorporating new evidence on radiotherapy techniques and target-volume de-escalation, chemotherapy regimens and their sequencing, adjuvant therapy, and immunotherapy for patients with stage IB-III disease.
METHODS: A multidisciplinary Expert Panel reviewed evidence published since the prior guideline, including randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant prospective and retrospective studies. Outcomes of interest included overall survival, failure-free or progression-free survival, locoregional and distant disease control, acute and late toxicities, and patient-reported quality of life. Recommendations were developed using the ASCO guideline development process and Expert Panel consensus.
RESULTS: The updated evidence supports: IMRT with image guidance and MRI-based target delineation as core components of definitive treatment; selected response-adapted target delineation following induction chemotherapy; elective nodal de-escalation in appropriately selected patients; risk-adapted chemotherapy sequencing according to stage and biologic risk; cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy; gemcitabine-cisplatin (GP) or docetaxel-cisplatin-fluorouracil (TPF) as preferred induction regimens; and selected adjuvant chemotherapy options, including metronomic capecitabine for patients with higher residual post-chemoradiotherapy risk. Several randomized trials evaluating PD-1 inhibitors have demonstrated improved disease-control outcomes, but overall survival data remain immature.
RECOMMENDATIONS: This guideline update provides recommendations on radiotherapy technique, dose, imaging, and target delineation; sequencing of additional chemotherapy with radiotherapy; concurrent chemotherapy options; induction chemotherapy regimens and timing; adjuvant chemotherapy options; and the role of immunotherapy. At present, the Panel makes no recommendation for or against routine addition of immunotherapy to induction-concurrent chemoradiotherapy; applicability of the trial evidence, benefits and harms, local approval and access, and patient preferences should guide individualized decisions.Additional information is available at www.ascopubs.org/topics/asco-guidelines/head-neck-cancer.

43003078.title: Decoding neutrophil spatial heterogeneity and clinical implications in breast cancer.
43003078.author: Xu YZ
43003078.abstract: Neutrophils are heterogeneous and critical components of the tumor microenvironment, yet their spatial heterogeneity and clinical implications remain poorly understood. We establish large-scale breast cancer cohorts integrating AI-powered computational pathology (n = 1,113) and single-cell spatial omics (n = 104) to investigate the clinical relevance and biological mechanisms underlying neutrophil spatial patterns. Clinical implications were greatest in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC): neutrophil-tumor cell proximity associated with favorable prognosis, while neutrophil-immune cell proximity predicted superior immunotherapy response. Combining these patterns with established biomarkers improved TNBC stratification for prognosis and immunotherapy efficacy. Spatial omics and experimental validation demonstrated that tumor-proximal neutrophils enhanced MHC I expression on tumor cells via inflammatory crosstalk, promoting immune-mediated tumor clearance and improved prognosis. Neutrophils adjacent to immune cells exhibited an antigen-presenting phenotype, augmentable by targeting polyamine metabolism. Our study highlights the functional diversity and spatial heterogeneity of neutrophils and provides a translational strategy with routine computational pathology.

43003076.title: Neutrophils are known by their neighbors in breast cancer.
43003076.author: Pei S
43003076.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Xu et al. combine large-scale computational pathology, spatial omics, and functional experiments to examine neutrophil organization in triple-negative breast tumors. They identify two neutrophil niches with different clinical associations: tumor-proximal neutrophils are linked to favorable prognosis, whereas neutrophils near immune cells associate with immunotherapy response.

43019709.title: Mapping the overlap of predictive biomarkers in an advanced Austrian multicenter gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma real-world cohort - results from the AGMT GASTRIC-5 registry.
43019709.author: Huemer F
43019709.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The predictive biomarker landscape and first-line treatment strategies for advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma are rapidly evolving. However, the co-occurrence of biomarkers in Western patient populations has not been comprehensively described.
METHODS: This extended biomarker analysis of the AGMT GASTRIC-5 Registry aimed to evaluate predictive biomarker prevalence and overlaps in an advanced, Austrian, multicenter gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma real-world cohort. All analyses were centrally performed in a pathology reference laboratory by a single experienced observer.
RESULTS: Between 2011 and 2018, 100 patients with quantitatively and qualitatively sufficient tumor samples were eligible for retrospective biomarker assessment. Biomarker frequencies were as follows: mismatch-repair-deficient: 6%; HER2-positive: 22%; HER2-low: 51%; HER2-zero (IHC 0): 27%; PD-L1 CPS ≥ 1: 77%, ≥ 5: 44%, and ≥ 10: 33%; PD-L1 TAP score ≥ 1%: 75%, ≥ 5%: 49%, and ≥ 10%: 33%; CLDN18.2-positive: 41% overall and 42% among HER2-zero/HER2-low tumors; and FGFR2b-positive: 4%. The overlap between PD-L1 CPS-positive and CLDN18.2-positive cases among mismatch-repair-proficient & HER2-zero/HER2-low patients was 31% for CPS ≥ 1, 13% for CPS ≥ 5, and 10% for CPS ≥ 10, respectively. Concurrent negativity for PD-L1 CPS, CLDN18.2, HER2, and mismatch-repair status was observed in 11% of patients using a PD-L1 CPS cutoff of < 1, in 25% using a cutoff of < 5, and in 29% using a cutoff of < 10.
CONCLUSION: This extended biomarker analysis of the AGMT GASTRIC-5 Registry provides detailed centrally-assessed, single-observer data on established predictive biomarkers and those under investigation in advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma at the patient level. The reported biomarker frequencies, expression patterns, and overlap profiles may support the design of future testing strategies and biomarker-driven clinical trials.
