43013899.title: Indole-3-lactic acid ameliorates thrombocytopenia in primary immune thrombocytopenia by modulating the differentiation of Th17 and Tregs.
43013899.author: Zhan Y
43013899.abstract: Although some patients with primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) benefit from current treatments, there are still some refractory patients. Our previous research showed that the imbalance of the intestinal microbiota is associated with ITP. Indole-3-lactic acid (ILA) may act as a communication channel between the gut microbiota and the immune system. This study aimed to assess the ILA metabolism and the role in ITP. Plasma metabolites were measured by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Flow cytometry was used to analyse T-cell subsets and Fc gamma receptors on macrophages. Cytokine mRNA expression and plasma levels were detected by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and a multiplex assay kit. An ITP mouse model was used to explore the effect of ILA on immune homeostasis. Newly diagnosed and refractory ITP patients with a deficiency of ILA and an imbalance of T helper cell type 17 (Th17)/regulatory T cells (Tregs). ILA alleviated thrombocytopenia in ITP mice by inhibiting Th17 differentiation and the expression of interleukin (IL)-1β, tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and IL-12/IL-23p40, and by promoting Tregs differentiation. ILA reduced Th17 cells, increased the Treg/Th17 ratio, downregulated IL17A and TNFα mRNA, and upregulated IL10 mRNA in refractory ITP patients. ILA ameliorates thrombocytopenia in ITP by modulating Th17/Tregs differentiation and suppressing TNF-α expression. Targeting ILA metabolism could be a promising therapeutic strategy for ITP.

43022425.title: Differential platelet-derived extracellular vesicle signatures in preeclampsia with and without intrauterine growth restriction.
43022425.author: Carvalho V
43022425.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Preeclampsia toxemia (PET) and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) are major complications of pregnancy, both characterized by vascular dysfunction and dysregulated hemostasis. Despite overlapping pathophysiology, robust biomarkers that distinguish these clinical phenotypes remain limited. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), particularly those derived from platelets and endothelial cells, have emerged as mediators and potential biomarkers of thromboinflammatory processes in pregnancy.
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether circulating EV profiles differ between gestational age-matched pregnancies with isolated PET and those with PET complicated by IUGR.
METHODS: We conducted a gestational age-matched cross-sectional analysis nested within a prospective cohort of pregnant patients with PET. Eighty-six participants were included: isolated PET (n = 63) and PET complicated by IUGR (n = 23). Circulating EVs were characterized using nanoparticle tracking analysis and flow cytometry to assess vesicle size, concentration, and cellular origin. Statistical comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U-test in RStudio.
RESULTS: Circulating phosphatidylserine (PS)+/CD41+/CD42b-/CD62P+ platelet-derived EVs were significantly increased in PET with IUGR compared with isolated PET. Total EV concentration and mode size of small EVs did not differ significantly between groups. The EV profile observed in PET with IUGR is consistent with enhanced platelet activation and a procoagulant phenotype in the maternal circulation, potentially reflecting a systemic hemostatic perturbation associated with placental dysfunction.
CONCLUSION: Circulating activated platelet-derived EV profiles differentiate PET with and without IUGR. These findings support a role for EVs as biomarkers of maternal hypercoagulability and suggest their utility in stratifying clinically relevant subtypes of preeclampsia.

43031912.title: Interassay and interlaboratory comparison of von Willebrand factor antigen as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker in advanced chronic liver disease.
43031912.author: Balcar L
43031912.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Von Willebrand factor antigen (VWF:Ag) is an inexpensive assay that is broadly available in diagnostic laboratories. The ratio of von Willebrand factor antigen and platelet count (VITRO) score (VWF:Ag/platelet count ratio) is the most promising blood-based test for clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH) in compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD). However, most published data are based on the Stago VWF:Ag assay. To allow widespread clinical application, we performed a comparative study with other commonly used assays.
METHODS: We included 353 patients with cACLD and decompensated cirrhosis undergoing hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement. Frozen citrated plasma samples were provided to centers with expertise in hemostasis and coagulation tests applying different assays (ie, Stago-Groningen, Werfen/IL-Padova, and Siemens-Lausanne).
RESULTS: Mean differences between VWF:Ag and VITRO levels of Stago vs Siemens were 49.6 (95% CI, 43.9-55.3) % vs 0.59 (95% CI, 0.51-0.67) and between those of Stago vs Werfen/IL were 12.1 (95% CI, 5.7-18.5) % vs 0.18 (95% CI, 0.10-0.26). Stago and Werfen/IL (intraclass correlation, 0.911; r, 0.914) as well as Siemens (intraclass correlation, 0.921; r, 0.922) showed near perfect correlation. Systematically lower VWF:Ag values by the Siemens assay are amendable by a newly developed conversion formula for patients with ACLD. Among patients with cACLD and Child-Turcotte-Pugh stage A, VITRO scores yielded consistently high areas under the curve (Stago: 0.865; Werfen/IL: 0.865; Siemens: 0.855). Using the previously established VITRO score cutoff of ≥2.5 to rule in CSPH, the positive predictive value was >90% with all assays.
CONCLUSION: Our head-to-head comparison indicates that the widespread introduction of VWF:Ag and VITRO score into clinical practice may rely on existing infrastructure, as commonly used diagnostic assays either yielded consistent, or in case of Siemens, easily convertible results. For ruling-in CSPH in cACLD by VITRO, no conversion is required.

43032906.title: Impact of the Lebanese Crisis on the Treatment of Patients With Haemophilia and von Willebrand Disease.
43032906.author: Charbel N
43032906.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Haemophilia and von Willebrand disease (VWD) are inherited bleeding disorders requiring lifelong access to haemostatic therapies and coordinated multidisciplinary care. Lebanon's prolonged economic and healthcare crises have disrupted medication supply, financing, and access to specialized services, creating particular challenges for individuals with rare bleeding disorders.
AIM: To evaluate how Lebanon's prolonged economic and healthcare crises affected treatment access, care delivery, and health-system support for patients with haemophilia and VWD.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative review incorporating a retrospective descriptive analysis of aggregated data from the Lebanese Association for Haemophilia (LAH) beneficiary registry and programmatic records, complemented by World Federation of Hemophilia data and published literature. The principal longitudinal LAH dataset covered 2019-2023, with updated beneficiary-registry data through 2026.
RESULTS: The number of individuals recorded in the LAH beneficiary registry increased from 458 in 2019 to 547 in 2023 and reached 591 by June 2026. Reliance on humanitarian treatment support increased substantially during the crisis. Recorded donated-product quantities rose from 873,262 units in 2019 to 4,002,211 in 2022, representing a 4.58-fold increase (+358.3%), before declining to 2,459,558 in 2023. By 2026, LAH programmatic data indicated partial recovery in factor VIII and IX availability and expansion of non-factor therapy, including emicizumab, although shortages persisted for selected VWD and rare bleeding-disorder therapies.
CONCLUSION: Lebanon's overlapping crises substantially disrupted haemophilia and VWD care and increased reliance on LAH and humanitarian assistance. Although treatment availability has partially improved, important gaps remain. Sustainable progress will require reliable national financing and procurement, coordinated registry systems, and prospective clinical-outcome monitoring.

43032895.title: Development of Haemophilia Specialist Nurses and Current Status Survey of Nursing Practice in China.
43032895.author: Zhang W
43032895.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Little is known about the breadth of nursing practice and its determinants among haemophilia specialist nurses in China.
AIM: To review the evolution of haemophilia specialist nursing in China and investigate the current status and key determinants of nursing practice.
METHODS: A national cross-sectional survey was conducted among haemophilia specialist nurses across 27 provincial level regions. A self-designed questionnaire collected data on demographics, work characteristics, and participation rates across seven practice domains. Multivariate logistic regression identified independent predictors of higher practice level.
RESULTS: Among 131 nurses, health education for patients/families achieved the highest participation rate (93.3%), with infusion education (98.5%) and bleeding assessment (97.7%) near universal. Extended care (60.5%) and research (66.4%) were lowest, 35.1% had never participated in research. Four independent predictors were identified: proportion of working time allocated to haemophilia (OR = 1.027, 95% CI: 1.005-1.049), weekly overtime hours for haemophilia care (OR = 1.634, 95% CI: 1.057-2.525), number of patients in the centre (OR = 1.786, 95% CI: 1.185-2.693), and dedicated non-clinical time (OR = 5.857, 95% CI: 1.132-30.283).
CONCLUSION: Haemophilia specialist nursing in China has progressed substantially in patient education, yet research and extended care remain weak. The absence of formalised nursing posts and protected non-clinical time is the most critical structural barrier. Establishing designated posts for hemophilia nursing practice should be prioritised.

43009022.title: Sepsis in Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell Therapy: A Six-Year Nationwide Analysis of Clinical Outcomes and Healthcare Resource Utilization in Hospitalizations for Hematologic Malignancies.
43009022.author: Mohammad A
43009022.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients receiving chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy are at increased risk for infection and sepsis due to malignancy-related immune dysfunction, lymphodepleting chemotherapy, and immunosuppression used to treat CAR T-cell toxicities; however, nationally representative estimates of sepsis burden and economic impact remain limited.
OBJECTIVES: This study uses nationally representative U.S. data to evaluate patient characteristics, clinical outcomes, and healthcare utilization associated with sepsis among hospitalizations involving CAR T-cell therapy.
STUDY DESIGN: Adult hospitalizations for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or multiple myeloma in which CAR T-cell therapy was administered between 2017 and 2022 were identified from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) and stratified by sepsis status. After excluding records with missing covariates, survey-weighted analyses were performed to generate nationally representative estimates. Multivariable regression models were used to evaluate differences in mortality and secondary outcomes, with statistical significance defined as a two-sided p value < 0.05.
RESULTS: Among 10,450 weighted CAR T-cell therapy hospitalizations, 645 (6.2%) were complicated by sepsis. In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in hospitalizations with sepsis (28.7% vs 1.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 33.96; 95% confidence interval [CI] 18.67-61.75). Sepsis was independently associated with higher odds of acute kidney injury (aOR 4.31), respiratory failure (aOR 11.85), acute hepatic failure (aOR 44.42), and septic shock (aOR 411.05), along with greater use of renal replacement therapy, mechanical ventilation, and vasopressors. Thrombohemorrhagic events were more frequent among hospitalizations with sepsis, including disseminated intravascular coagulation (aOR 9.30), acute venous thromboembolism (aOR 2.95), acute coronary syndrome (aOR 27.63), acute ischemic stroke (aOR 7.53), gastrointestinal hemorrhage (aOR 6.47), and intracranial hemorrhage (aOR 4.84), as well as increased need for cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma transfusion (aOR 2.70). Sepsis was also associated with longer hospital stay (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR] 1.96) and higher hospitalization charges (adjusted charge ratio [aCR] 1.22).
CONCLUSIONS: Sepsis was documented in approximately 6% of CAR T-cell hospitalizations and was associated with higher in-hospital mortality, organ dysfunction, critical-care utilization, longer hospitalization, and higher hospitalization charges. These findings highlight the substantial clinical and healthcare burden associated with sepsis in this population.

43034553.title: Feminizing and masculinizing gender-affirming hormone therapy have distinct effects on fibrinogen γ'.
43034553.author: Bøgehave M
43034553.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fibrinogen γ' is an alternatively spliced fibrinogen isoform. Higher fibrinogen γ' levels are associated with arterial thrombosis and lower levels with venous thrombosis. Feminizing gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT) increases venous thrombosis risk, whereas masculinizing GAHT increases arterial thrombosis risk. How GAHT affects fibrinogen γ' is unknown.
OBJECTIVES: We aimed to investigate changes in fibrinogen γ' levels after 12 months of feminizing or masculinizing GAHT.
METHODS: Fibrinogen γ' and total fibrinogen were measured at baseline and after 12 months of GAHT in 245 transgender women and 318 transgender men (cohort study). Feminizing GAHT included oral or transdermal estradiol combined with cyproterone acetate (CPA) (3 groups). Masculinizing GAHT included intramuscular or transdermal testosterone with or without progestin (7 groups). Fibrinogen γ' was measured by ELISA and total fibrinogen by nephelometry. Relative fibrinogen γ' levels were calculated as the fibrinogen γ'/total fibrinogen ratio.
RESULTS: Fibrinogen γ' increased during feminizing GAHT (588 vs 628 μg/mL, P < .001), while relative fibrinogen γ' levels decreased (0.23 vs 0.22, P < .01). The increase in fibrinogen γ' was most pronounced with oral estradiol plus CPA (P < .02), while the decrease in relative fibrinogen γ' levels was comparable between treatment groups of feminizing GAHT. Fibrinogen γ' decreased during masculinizing GAHT (698 vs 660 μg/mL, P < .001), while relative fibrinogen γ' levels remained unchanged. No between-group differences were observed for masculinizing GAHT.
CONCLUSION: Feminizing and masculinizing GAHT for 12 months had opposite effects on fibrinogen γ' levels. Only the reduction in relative fibrinogen γ' levels during feminizing GAHT may contribute to increased venous thrombosis risk.

43031860.title: Enabling artificial intelligence-driven blind joint ultrasound self-scans in hemophilia: an annotation protocol.
43031860.author: Michelsanti D
43031860.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early detection and management of joint bleeding are critical for preventing long-term joint damage in people with hemophilia. However, current practices often require healthcare professionals to assess bleeding, limiting patient autonomy and potentially leading to delayed or unnecessary treatment. Current literature primarily focuses on clinical protocols for ultrasound (US) imaging but lacks annotation protocols tailored for training artificial intelligence (AI) systems.
OBJECTIVES: To propose a structured annotation protocol to support the development of an AI-driven, ultraportable US system that enables people with hemophilia to perform self-guided scans of their joints, focusing specifically on the posterior recess of the elbow, anterior subquadricipital recess of the knee, and anterior recess of the ankle.
METHODS: The annotation protocol defines eight criteria to assess the appropriateness of US images and five levels for region-of-interest clarity. A pool of six readers rated US videos of elbows, knees, and ankles from 100 healthy subjects, and their annotations were analyzed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).
RESULTS: The application of the proposed protocol demonstrates moderate to good agreement based on the ICC when assessing the reliability of single ratings from individual readers (ICC(2,1) = 0.7643), with the knee exhibiting the highest reliability. When considering average ratings across multiple readers, we observe overall excellent reliability, with an ICC of 0.9075.
CONCLUSION: This annotation protocol supports the development of future AI-guided image-acquisition systems for joint self-scanning, marking a significant step toward at-home joint assessment for people with hemophilia. Future research should address the evaluation of the AI guidance system, patient-performed scanning, and diagnostic accuracy for hemarthrosis.

43022395.title: Alternative Lys277 cleavage modulates tissue plasminogen activator processing and fibrinolysis.
43022395.author: Lebatard S
43022395.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is secreted as a single-chain enzyme and converted to its canonical 2-chain form by cleavage at Arg275. Whether the adjacent Lys277 residue contributes to tPA activation and fibrinolytic function remains unclear.
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether Lys277 can serve as an alternative tPA cleavage site and whether Lys277-dependent processing is associated with altered fibrinolytic activity.
METHODS: We combined phylogenetic analysis of PLAT sequences from 645 gnathostome species, engineered human tPA mutants targeting Arg275 and/or Lys277, plasmin- and plasma-cleavage assays, Edman sequencing, amidolytic and fibrin-plasminogen zymography, plasma clot lysis assays, and rotational thromboelastometry.
RESULTS: Arg275 was highly conserved across species, whereas species with Arg275 substitutions almost invariably retained Lys277; snakes contained only the Lys277 site. Plasmin cleaved wild-type tPA at Arg275-Ile276, whereas Arg275-mutant tPA was cleaved at Lys277-Gly278; mutation of both residues prevented 2-chain tPA formation. Compared with wild-type single-chain tPA, Arg275 single mutants reduced 50% lysis of fibrin-rich plasma clots by 1.9- to 2.4-fold and accelerated fibrinolysis of blood clots. Human plasma generated tPA heavy-chain fragments from wild-type and Arg275-mutant tPA, but not from the Arg275/Lys277 double mutant, indicating cleavage at both sites under plasma conditions. Preparations enriched in Lys277-cleaved tPA showed greater blood clot lysis than those enriched in Arg275-cleaved tPA, with corrected fibrinolysis up to 2.8-fold higher.
CONCLUSION: These data support Lys277 as an evolutionarily conserved alternative tPA cleavage site that can generate a 2-chain isoform with distinct fibrinolytic properties in vitro and ex vivo.

43034566.title: Hemostatic function remains unaltered following therapeutic factor XIIa inhibition with garadacimab.
43034566.author: Cohn DM
43034566.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Activated factor XII (FXIIa) initiates the kallikrein-kinin system, which is dysregulated in hereditary angioedema (HAE), leading to overproduction of bradykinin, the key mediator of swelling in HAE. Garadacimab (an anti-FXIIa monoclonal antibody) was recently approved for HAE long-term prophylaxis. In previous publications, patients with congenital factor XII (FXII) deficiency reported no increased risk of bleeding. The effect of long-term FXIIa inhibition on hemostasis in individuals with increased bleeding risk is not fully understood.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the impact of FXIIa inhibition on hemostasis in patients with increased bleeding risk receiving garadacimab.
METHODS: Abnormal bleeding events were monitored and medically reviewed in patients with HAE (phase 2, pivotal phase 3, and phase 3 open-label extension [OLE] studies) who received garadacimab with or without concomitant anticoagulant/antiplatelet medications. Abnormal bleeding events were further evaluated in patients who underwent invasive surgical/medical procedures in the phase 3 OLE and by concurrent Standardized MedDRA Query analysis across HAE studies. Relevant laboratory markers were evaluated in the phase 3 OLE. Abnormal bleeding was also assessed in patients with severe COVID-19 (phase 2 study) who received garadacimab with or without concomitant anticoagulant/antiplatelet medications.
RESULTS: No garadacimab-related abnormal bleeding events were observed, including among patients who received concomitant anticoagulant/antiplatelet medications or underwent invasive surgical/medical procedures. Plasma coagulation assays reflected natural variation.
CONCLUSION: Garadacimab-mediated FXIIa inhibition had no impact on hemostasis in patients with HAE or COVID-19 and increased bleeding risk, consistent with patients with congenital FXII deficiency who report no bleeding phenotypes.

43013818.title: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement.
43013818.author: Pellegrini VD Jr
43013818.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Studies comparing aspirin with anticoagulants for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty have had conflicting results.
METHODS: In a comparative-effectiveness noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned patients undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty to receive aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days. The composite primary effectiveness outcome (death from any cause or symptomatic VTE) and primary safety outcome (bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction) were evaluated through 6 months in a blinded fashion. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference was 0.69 percentage points.
RESULTS: Among 18,883 participants who had undergone randomization, 15,317 (7214 with hip arthroplasty and 8103 with knee arthroplasty) were included in the primary per-protocol analysis. A primary effectiveness outcome event occurred in 77 of 6090 participants (1.26%) in the aspirin group, in 52 of 4231 (1.23%) in the warfarin group, and in 47 of 4996 (0.94%) in the rivaroxaban group; a primary safety outcome event occurred in 177 (2.91%), 142 (3.36%), and 174 (3.48%), respectively. In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.30 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.20 to 0.81); 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin (difference, 0.23 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.34 to 0.81); and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.03 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.57 to 0.63). Risks of a primary safety outcome event were 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin (difference, 0.68 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.41); 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin (difference, 0.77 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.58); and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin (difference, -0.02 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.89 to 0.85). Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results.
CONCLUSIONS: Aspirin prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty was not noninferior to rivaroxaban or warfarin with respect to death or symptomatic VTE. Warfarin and rivaroxaban were not noninferior to aspirin for safety. (Funded by the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute; PEPPER ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02810704.).

43032401.title: Clinical outcomes, anticoagulation practice patterns, and quality of life after cancer-associated pulmonary embolism: secondary outcomes of the Hydra randomized clinical trial.
43032401.author: Akerboom B
43032401.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite its high prevalence, practice-based data on management and outcomes after cancer-associated pulmonary embolism (PE) are scarce, and no studies have investigated quality of life.
OBJECTIVES: We aimed to evaluate clinical outcomes, anticoagulation practice patterns, and quality of life after cancer-associated PE.
METHODS: The Hydra randomized clinical trial assessed the safety of the YEARS algorithm versus computed tomography pulmonary angiography only to exclude acute PE in patients with cancer. Patients with PE at baseline or during 90-day follow-up were included in this study. Outcomes were recurrent venous thromboembolism, major bleeding, all-cause mortality, anticoagulation practice patterns, and quality of life as assessed by the Pulmonary Embolism Quality of Life (PEmb-QoL) questionnaire. PEmb-QoL scores were compared with those for the general PE population reported in the FOCUS study. Lower scores indicate better QoL.
RESULTS: A total of 125 patients were included, of which 103 (82%) had PE at baseline, and 22 (18%) developed PE during follow-up. The 90-day cumulative incidence of recurrent venous thromboembolism and major bleeding was 2.5% (95% CI 0.67%-6.6%) and 2.5% (95% CI 0.68%-6.7%), respectively. All-cause mortality at 90 days was 32% (95% CI 23%-40%). Two-thirds of patients continued anticoagulation until less than 24 hours before death, and the median time between stopping anticoagulation and death was 10 days (IQR, 4-14). The median 90-day PEmb-QoL score was 33% (IQR, 13-51) versus 20% (IQR, 10-40) reported in the FOCUS study.
CONCLUSION: Patients with cancer-associated PE suffer from high mortality, high morbidity, and impaired quality of life. Anticoagulation therapy is frequently continued until the last days of life.

43031910.title: Characteristics of pediatric central venous catheter malfunction and subsequent catheter-related deep vein thrombosis.
43031910.author: Bala NS
43031910.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Central venous catheters (CVCs) are increasingly placed in children; however, malfunction and deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are reasons for frequent removal.
OBJECTIVES: The objective of this study was to evaluate variables associated with CVC malfunction and, subsequently, the development of CVC-related DVT (CR-DVT).
METHODS: This subanalysis of the multicenter, prospective Clot Incidence Rates in Central Lines study enrolled children aged 6 months to <18 years with newly placed peripherally inserted central catheters or tunneled lines from 2013 to 2018. Time from CVC placement to first malfunction was analyzed in the full cohort using univariable and multivariable Weibull regression. Among CVCs that malfunctioned, time from first malfunction to CR-DVT was analyzed to assess tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) use and subsequent thrombosis.
RESULTS: Malfunction occurred in 380/1951 CVCs (19.5%). In multivariable analysis, prior CVC use (hazard ratio [HR], 1.51; 95% CI, 1.19-1.90; P = .001), multilumen catheters (HR, 2.89; 95% CI, 2.30-3.65; P < .001), and >2 insertion attempts (HR, 2.21; 95% CI, 1.42-3.45; P < .001) were associated with a higher risk of malfunction, whereas catheter size >4 French and interventional radiology placement were associated with a lower risk. Among malfunctioning CVCs, 22/380 (5.8%) developed CR-DVT, with a median time to CR-DVT of 6 days after malfunction. Increasing t-PA use showed a nonsignificant trend toward higher subsequent CR-DVT.
CONCLUSION: CVC malfunction is common and associated with several modifiable catheter-related factors. Six percent of malfunctioning CVCs develop CR-DVT, and repeated t-PA use and persistent CVC dysfunction may warrant further evaluation for underlying thrombosis.

43032209.title: Multiplex complement profiling uncovers complement activation signatures in microvascular manifestations of antiphospholipid syndrome.
43032209.author: Cai B
43032209.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The 2023 American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) classification criteria define a clinical domain characterized mainly by microvascular thrombosis formation and is associated with complement activation.
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to evaluate the relationship between the complement profile and organ-specific manifestations of APS, especially microvascular APS (MAPS).
METHODS: Patients who fulfilled the 2023 ACR/EULAR APS classification criteria were enrolled. Plasma levels of complement components (Ba, Bb, C3a, C4a, C5a, soluble C5b-9, factor H, factor I, C1q, C2, C3, C4, C5, factor D, and factor P) were quantified by chemiluminescent multiplex enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Cluster analysis was performed to identify distinct complement activation profiles among clinical subgroups.
RESULTS: A total of 58 patients with APS, including 51 patients with MAPS consecutively enrolled between August 2023 and June 2025, and 20 healthy controls (HCs) were included in the study. Compared with HCs, patients with MAPS had significantly higher plasma levels of Ba, C3a, C4a, and sC5b-9, and significantly lower levels of C1q, C2, and factor P (all P < .05). Cluster analysis identified 3 subgroups: cluster 1 characterized by predominant MAPS manifestations with marked alternative pathway activation; cluster 2 enriched for myocardial disease and antinuclear antibody positivity, showing predominance of classical and lectin pathway activation; and cluster 3 characterized by macrovascular thrombosis with relatively mild complement activation. A predictive model combining factor P and C3a demonstrated good performance for MAPS (AUC = 0.898; sensitivity 82.4%; specificity 88.9%).
CONCLUSIONS: Complement profiling may serve as a valuable tool for early identification of MAPS, disease monitoring, and guiding individualized treatment, highlighting the potential of complement-targeted therapies in MAPS.

43031507.title: HLA-antibody testing female donors with a pregnancy history augments the low titer group O whole blood supply.
43031507.author: Jochumsen EA
43031507.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low titer group O whole blood (LTOWB) use across the United States is increasing. This simulation calculated the number of female donors who would qualify for LTOWB donation if HLA-antibody screening was implemented in different strategies.
METHODS: Using US nativity data and information on blood donors from 2023, a model was constructed that calculated how many of these donors would be males and nulliparous females, neither of which require HLA-antibody screening before LTOWB donation. The model then calculated how many parous females would be HLA-antibody sensitized based on each woman's parity in three antibody screening scenarios: all parous women, all parous women ≥50 years old, and all parous women older than the 99th percentile of the age of final birth. These calculations were performed for RhD-negative and RhD-positive donors.
RESULTS: The model calculated that there would be 222,239 RhD-negative male and 74,655 nulliparous RhD-negative female donors. If all group O RhD-negative parous females were screened, 109,479 were calculated to not be HLA-sensitized for a total of 406,373 LTOWB eligible donors. If only the group O RhD-negative females ≥50 years were screened, 59,138 donors would not be HLA-sensitized for a total of 356,032 LTOWB eligible donors. If only the group O RhD-negative females ≥42 years, the 99th percentile for last birth age, were screened, 80,375 donors would not be HLA-sensitized for a total of 377,269 LTOWB eligible donors. Higher numbers of LTOWB donors were realized when RhD-positive males and females were modeled.
CONCLUSION: HLA-antibody screening realizes additional LTOWB donors.

43023684.title: Evaluation of rare and novel splicing variants in the RH system.
43023684.author: Floch A
43023684.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Single nucleotide variants near intron/exon junctions can affect RNA splicing, resulting in weak or loss of blood group antigen expression. We investigated 11 samples with no causative variants found in RH coding exons: three with weak RhD phenotypes and 8 with discordance between phenotypes and DNA prediction for RhCE.
METHODS: Serologic and DNA testing was performed by standard methods. RH exons 1-10 and flanking introns were amplified and Sanger sequenced. Variants were evaluated using an in vitro splicing minigene assay.
RESULTS: Three weak D phenotypes were associated with intron 1, RHD*149-1G>A, or intron 3, RHD*487-3C>A or RHD*487-3C>G, variants. Splicing assay confirmed activation of a cryptic acceptor site for RHD*149-1A, and both RHD*487-3A and -3G resulted in mis-splicing with minor amounts of normal transcripts. Among eight RHCE discrepancies: three had an intron 4 variant, RHCE*Ce c.635-9G>A, causing a 7-bp insertion, frameshift/stop; five had other intron variants, RHCE*cE c.336-2A>G, RHCE*ce c.486+1G>A, RHCE*ce c.1154-1G>A, RHCE*Ce c.939+1G>A, showing complete splicing disruption, and RHCE*Ce c.148+5G>T with no splicing disruption detectable.
CONCLUSIONS: Alleles studied here had intron variants associated with weak or absence of detectable antigen expression. Five are null alleles, RHCE*Ce635-9A, RHCE*ce486+1A, RHCE*ce1154-1A, RHCE*Ce148+5T, and RHCE*Ce939+1A, while RHCE*cE336-2G is associated with E antigen detected by adsorption/elution. Splicing assays support RHD*149-1A may encode an altered RhD, while the low level of normal splicing shown for RHD*487-3A and RHD*487-3G suggests very weak expression but the absence of alloimmunization risk. The minigene splicing assay offers insight into the effect of intron variants on antigen expression.

43015961.title: Recipient and donor contact following unrelated allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation: The Canadian Blood Services' stem cell registry experience.
43015961.author: Duong A
43015961.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Communication between recipients and their unrelated donors following hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) presents an important aspect of human connection that remains underreported. Characterizing recipient-donor contact within the Canadian Blood Services Stem Cell Registry (CBS SCR) and summarizing international registry policies provides a novel perspective on HCT care.
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Recipient-donor contact requests directed to the CBS SCR between 2022 and 2024 were analyzed. Policies concerning anonymous and direct recipient-donor contact from international donor registries accredited by the world marrow donor association (WMDA) were retrieved and compared.
RESULTS: A total of 325 recipient-donor contact requests were submitted to CBS SCR during the study period, representing 18.6% of implicated unrelated donor transplants. Most commonly, requests (79%, n = 257) involved an international donor and Canadian recipient, and 62% (n = 202) were initiated by recipients or their families. There were 83 (26%) unsuccessful contact requests (52, or 63% initiated by donors). Recipient death was the most common reason for an unsuccessful contact request (n = 32, 39%). Anonymous contact between recipients and donors is permissible by 58 of 64 (91%) international registries that provided policy information to WMDA, while direct contact is permitted by 28 (44%) after a period ranging from 1 to 5 years.
DISCUSSION: Our findings highlight significant interest in recipient-donor communication and contact. We identified significant variability across international registry policies. We recommend a simplified and standardized policy that could increase successful recipient donor communication and augment visibility that could be leveraged to enhance recruitment of motivated potential donors.

43015073.title: Digital connectivity in plateletpheresis collections improves productivity and workflow efficiency without compromising donor safety.
43015073.author: de Almeida-Neto C
43015073.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Blood banks face pressure to meet the growing demand for platelet components while improving operational efficiency and maintaining donor and patient safety. This study describes a data-driven strategy using connectivity tools to reduce data transfer errors, optimize workflow, and safely implement high-yield platelet collections.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective observational study analyzed plateletpheresis procedures performed with Trima Accel™ Automated Blood Collection System between January 2022 and November 2025 at Fundação Pró-Sangue, São Paulo. In November 2022, the Terumo Operational Medical Equipment Software (TOMEs™) middleware was implemented to establish a bidirectional interface between apheresis devices and the blood bank information system. Data-driven simulations identified donors eligible for high-yield collections, enabling the introduction of triple-dose plateletpheresis in October 2024. Variables included donor data discrepancies, adverse events, procedure duration, platelet yield, predicted post-procedure platelet counts, anticoagulant use, inter-donation intervals, and workflow efficiency. Outcomes before and after implementation were compared.
RESULTS: Integration of the bidirectional interface reduced donor data discrepancies from 47% to 3%, and decreased manual interactions by 30%, improving data reliability and operational efficiency. Simulations showed that 30% of donors met Brazilian regulatory criteria for triple-dose plateletpheresis. After implementation, plateletpheresis productivity increased 16%. Adverse event rates remained low and comparable before and after implementation (8.2% vs. 7.9%). Predicted post-procedure platelet counts in triple donors remained within the device safety threshold recommended by Brazilian policies.
CONCLUSION: Digital integration and data-driven decision-making enable the safe implementation of triple-dose plateletpheresis, improving productivity without compromising donor safety. This approach may serve as a practical model for blood centers, particularly in resource-limited settings.

43004897.title: Development of a novel manufacturing process for highly purified and stable immunoglobulin M with enhanced plasma utilization.
43004897.author: Xia WR
43004897.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Immunoglobulin M (IgM) is a promising therapeutic agent. However, its production is limited by high molecular weight, complex structure and poor stability. This study aimed to develop a novel manufacturing process for high-purity, stable plasma-derived IgM while improving plasma utilization.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The flow-through fraction from first-step anion-exchange chromatography (Step 1 AEX) in an intravenous immunoglobulin manufacturing process was used as the starting material. Second-step AEX (Step 2 AEX) and third-step mixed-mode chromatography (Step 3 MMC) were used to remove impurities, including prekallikrein activator (PKA), immunoglobulin G (IgG), immunoglobulin A (IgA) and α2-macroglobulin. The elution conditions for Step 2 AEX were optimized to improve IgM recovery and purity. Four resins were evaluated for Step 3 MMC, and separation conditions were optimized to increase IgM purity and recovery. Finally, formulation studies were conducted to improve IgM stability.
RESULTS: The optimized conditions were stepwise elution for Step 2 AEX (0.4 M followed by 1.0 M sodium acetate), Capto Core 400 resin for flow-through-mode Step 3 MMC and loading at pH 7.8, conductivity 15.0 mS/cm and protein concentration 1.0% (w/v). Key impurities IgA and PKA were reduced to 0.184 ± 0.011 mg/mL and below the limit of detection (<10 IU/mL), respectively, and IgM purity exceeded 90%. Under the final formulation conditions (0.1 M glycine, pH 4.0), the high-purity IgM showed good stability.
CONCLUSION: A novel process was developed to address the critical challenges in plasma-derived IgM manufacture, achieving high IgM purity (>90%). By optimizing plasma utilization, this process represents a promising platform for next-generation immunoglobulin therapies.

43004657.title: Novel fluorescent interference preventing peripheral CD34+ cell enumeration in a healthy, mobilized hematopoietic progenitor cell apheresis donor.
43004657.author: Potter S
43004657.abstract:
CASE PRESENTATION: A 34-year-old healthy related male allogeneic stem cell donor showed apparent mobilization failure. The recipient, the donor's mother, received a haploidentical conditioning regimen, but total body irradiation was delayed as a result. Stem cell collection was initiated while investigation for pre-analytical and analytical laboratory error for CD34 cell enumeration was conducted. Clerical checks and repeat CD34 cell enumeration studies showed no discrepancies. Peripheral smears showed appropriate leukocytosis with prominent left shift. On review, flow cytometry plots demonstrated a shift from baseline in fluorescence intensity of background leukocytes in the CD34-phycoerythrin channel obscuring a CD34+ cell population suggesting interference. A preanalytical saline wash resolved the interference. The final yield of the collected product was 16.2 × 106 CD34+ cells/kg recipient weight without evidence of interference. The recipient received irradiation, stem cells were infused, and successfully engrafted on Day 17, remaining in molecular remission 6 months post-transplant.
DISCUSSION: Potential interference mechanisms in flow cytometry assays include autofluorescence and non-specific antibody binding. Possible interfering substances for consideration included cannabinoids, riboflavin, turmeric extract, and other compounds which may be present in marijuana edible gummies, which were disclosed by the donor during in-depth history evaluation. Intraprocedural dilution, selective separation during apheresis, and pre-analytical dilution likely eliminated the interference when testing the stem cell product.
CONCLUSION: Suspected mobilization failure may be due to interference/laboratory error. Sample dilution and washing may resolve interferences. In time-sensitive cases, systematic investigation to rule out common causes of laboratory error is essential to avoid delays in patient care.

43003081.title: Transfusion-transmitted malaria in Europe and North America: Epidemiology, residual risk and implications for blood safety policies.
43003081.author: La Raja M
43003081.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Transfusion-transmitted malaria (TTM) is a rare but potentially severe transfusion complication. Increasing global mobility from malaria-endemic regions challenges donor selection policies in non-endemic settings, as asymptomatic parasitaemia may persist for years in previously exposed semi-immune individuals. This review aims to contextualise the residual risk of TTM and critically appraise current and past preventive strategies considering available evidence, with particular attention to policy implications.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A literature review of all confirmed cases of TTM reported in Europe and North America between 2005 and 2024 was performed to retrospectively assess the effectiveness and limitations of past and current preventive strategies, with particular reference to the recommendations of the European Directorate for the Quality of Medicines & HealthCare (EDQM) Blood Guide and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
RESULTS: Eighteen confirmed TTM cases were identified: 11 by Plasmodium falciparum with three fatalities, six by Plasmodium malariae and one by Plasmodium ovale. Sixteen cases were linked to donors born in or long-term residents of malaria-endemic regions, predominantly sub-Saharan Africa; two involved short-term European travellers. Since 2012, no P. falciparum TTM cases have been reported in Europe following the correct implementation of EDQM guidelines.
CONCLUSION: The residual risk of TTM in Europe and North America appears to be extremely low. However, long-term asymptomatic carriers-particularly of P. falciparum-remain a potential threat. Approaches based on deferral and immunological testing appeared to be effective and sustainable; nevertheless, high-sensitivity nucleic acid testing may represent a valuable alternative, particularly where blood availability is critical.

43000646.title: Utilization of blood in patients with gunshot wounds: A Canadian single-center experience.
43000646.author: Tabatabaey A
43000646.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Blood product utilization among gunshot wound (GSW) victims has not been characterized in Canada. This study describes transfusion requirements in GSW patients treated at a major Canadian Level-1 urban trauma center.
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: A retrospective review of a hospital trauma registry in Toronto, Canada, identified GSW patients between 2017 and 2021. Patients under 16, those refusing transfusions, and patients with Absent Vital Signs for whom resuscitation was not initiated were excluded. Total and component-specific transfusions of red blood cells (RBC), plasma, and platelets were analyzed across hospital stay.
RESULTS: Of 5452 trauma team activations, 5% were GSWs (n = 275; 91.3% male, n = 251; median age 26; overall mortality 14.9%, n = 41). Overall, 77 patients (28%) received 1134 units of blood components while 198 patients (72%) did not require any transfusions. Among those who required transfusions, the average number of blood product units (RBC, plasma, and platelets combined) per patient was 14.47. Transfusions included 716 RBC units, 344 plasma units, and 74 platelet pools. Consumption was markedly skewed: 18 patients (6.5%) who required at least 10 units consumed 70.5% of RBCs, 3.3% (n = 9) received 72.7% of plasma, and 1.1% (n = 3) used 59.5% of platelets.
DISCUSSION: In this 5-year review, although GSWs account for a minority of trauma activations, they exert a disproportionate demand on blood inventory, driven heavily by an extreme minority of severely injured patients. Increasing gun violence may further strain the blood supply and recognition of this concentrated utilization pattern is essential for blood bank inventory preparedness, clinical care pathways, and injury prevention strategies.

43034110.title: The Effect of Different Images Watched With Virtual Reality on Perception Pain and Anxiety During Phlebotomy: A Randomized Controlled Study.
43034110.author: Karaman D
43034110.abstract: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of viewing cold-themed and hot-themed VR environments on pain and anxiety during phlebotomy in first-time voluntary whole-blood donors. This prospective, randomized controlled study was conducted with first-time voluntary whole-blood donors. Participants were allocated to the VR-Cold Themed group, the VR-Hot Themed group, and the control group, each comprising 40 participants, using a block randomization method. Data were collected using the Descriptive Characteristics Form, Visual Analog Scale (VAS), and State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI). After phlebotomy, the mean pain scores were 0.85 ± 0.44 in the VR-Cold Themed group, 2.35 ± 0.55 in the VR-Hot Themed group, and 5.20 ± 0.74 in the control group. The mean anxiety scores were 28.42 ± 7.24, 29.22 ± 5.93, and 40.22 ± 11.98, respectively. Pain scores were significantly lower in the VR-Cold Themed group than in the VR-Hot Themed and control groups (P < .001). Anxiety scores were significantly lower in both VR groups than in the control group (P < .001), with no significant difference between the 2 VR groups (P = .913). Among first-time voluntary whole-blood donors, viewing the VR-Cold Themed environment was associated with lower pain levels than viewing the VR-Hot Themed environment or undergoing the standard phlebotomy procedure. Viewing both VR environments was associated with lower phlebotomy-related anxiety levels than the standard phlebotomy procedure.

43015238.title: CD36 Deficiency in Platelet Donors and Clinical Transfusion Practice: A Comprehensive Critical Review of Key Molecular, Epidemiological, and Translational Studies.
43015238.author: Shen TC
43015238.abstract: CD36 deficiency demonstrates higher frequency among East Asian populations and is closely associated with alloimmunization risk. This critical review systematically evaluates 6 landmark studies that have advanced understanding of CD36 deficiency, including its epidemiological characteristics in Chinese and Japanese populations, molecular mechanisms involving genomic-complementary DNA (cDNA) discordance, alternative splicing, regulatory haplotypes, messenger RNA (mRNA) expression and soluble CD36 as a potential biomarker, as well as clinical correlations with transfusion-related adverse events. Scientific strengths, methodological limitations and generalizability of each study were comprehensively assessed. The results demonstrate distinct ethnic genetic differentiation of CD36 deficiency caused by recurrent variants, noncoding regulatory variations and alternative splicing, with clear genotype-transcript divergence distinguishing type I and type II deficiency. Major strengths include large cohorts, rigorous flow cytometric phenotyping and high-resolution sequencing; limitations include regional bias, limited prospective follow-up and incomplete mechanisms of platelet-specific CD36 silencing. Critical gaps remain in lineage-specific regulation, standardized screening and multiethnic genetics. Future research should focus on multi-center prospective cohorts, long-read sequencing, functional validation and clinical guidelines to reduce transfusion complications. This review offers translational insights for both basic research and clinical transfusion practice.

43020704.title: Donor Willingness and Participation in Health and Genetic Screening Within Blood Banks: A Narrative Review.
43020704.author: Marx LJH
43020704.abstract: Blood banks increasingly offer additional health and genomic screening alongside routine donation, providing donors with personalized results. This review aims to assess the available evidence on donors' willingness to participate in additional screening and the behavioral outcomes following receipt of the results. We conducted a systematic search in Embase, PubMed, and Web of Science (February-March 2026) using predefined search terms and clear inclusion criteria. We identified 9 relevant studies. From the eligible studies, we selected 5 articles for review that had the highest relevance to the research questions and offered complementary perspectives across genetic, metabolic, and cardiovascular screening modalities. Donors expressed a high willingness to participate in additional screening when it was supported by trust in the blood bank and clarity about the screening's voluntary and secondary nature. Donors emphasized that receiving personal or genomic results should remain secondary to helping patients, in order to preserve the altruistic gift‑relationship that motivates donation. Behavioral actions, such as seeking care, making lifestyle changes, and discussing results with family, occurred mainly when donors received and understood their results. Clear communication and follow‑up procedures functioned as an underlying mechanism that supported both participation and appropriate action. As additional screening becomes integrated into blood donation practice, effective communication and supportive follow-up procedures are essential to promote informed participation and appropriate health-related action.

43017577.title: Modulation of the RNA-sensing RIG/MAVS pathway bypasses resistance to hypomethylating agents in acute myeloid leukemia.
43017577.author: El Khawanky N
43017577.abstract: DNA hypomethylating agents (HMAs) such as 5-azacytidine (5-AZA) are a cornerstone in the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), but development of resistance represents a major clinical challenge. Apart from epigenetic reprogramming of malignant cell clones, therapy with HMA is increasingly recognized to facilitate antineoplastic immunity, yet the relevance of these molecular mechanisms in AML remains poorly defined. Here, we show that AML cell-intrinsic sensing of aberrant RNA via the innate receptor system retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS) is essential for the therapeutic activity of HMAs. In human and murine AML cell lines, HMA treatment induced robust RIG-I/MAVS pathway activation and subsequent Type I interferon (IFN-I) release. HMA enhanced transcriptional activity of endogenous retroviral (ERV) elements that readily bound to the RIG-I receptor. Analysis of a small series of patient samples linked treatment response to elevated gene expression of ERV and RIG-I/MAVS pathway components in CD34+ cells including AML blasts. AML-intrinsic genetic ablation of MAVS or RIG-I abrogated the HMA treatment effects in mice by interfering with host IFN-I signaling and subsequent expansion and accumulation of activated T cells. Acquired HMA resistance was associated with ERV suppression and blunted RIG-I/MAVS signaling. Treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) restored RIG-I pathway activity and antileukemic response in mice bearing HMA-resistant AML. Our findings not only delineate a critical link between epigenetic modulation and innate immune activation in AML but also provide a rationale for targeting the RIG-I/MAVS RNA-sensing pathway to enhance antileukemic immunity and bypass epigenetic resistance to HMA.

43010832.title: NPM1-mutated AML: One entity, multiple layers of heterogeneity.
43010832.author: Meggendorfer M
43010832.abstract: Nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) mutations are found in around one third of all acute myeloid leukaemias (AMLs). However, little is known about the clinical role of the rare, non-A NPM1 variants. Sangiorgio et al. showed that rare variants shared a similar molecular background and overall survival to the common type A, with FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3) status as the main determinant of outcome. Commentary on: Sangiorgio et al. Rare variants of NPM1 mutations share a similar molecular background to the common NPM1 type A variant and are associated with similar survival in adults with acute myeloid leukaemia. 43008230.title: Pivekimab sunirine and the evolving treatment of blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm.
43008230.author: Beeler JS
43008230.abstract: Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) is a rare hematologic malignancy characterized by leukemic blasts with frequent cutaneous involvement and high CD123 expression. Pivekimab sunirine, an anti-CD123 antibody-drug conjugate with a DNA-alkylating payload, was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration on May 27, 2026, for adults with BPDCN based on the CADENZA study. We review its mechanism, clinical efficacy, toxicity, and role in the evolving treatment landscape for BPDCN and AML.

43025810.title: When cord blood grafts may be the preferred donor choice: a position statement from the ASTCT Cord Blood Special Interest Group.
43025810.author: Fingrut WB
43025810.abstract: The introduction and wide adoption of post-transplant cyclophosphamide-based graft-versus host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis has changed the landscape of allograft donor selection such that allograft candidates now commonly have multiple potential graft sources, and there can be uncertainty over which graft source to prioritize. This position statement, written by the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy Cord Blood (CB) Special Interest Group and leading CB transplant physicians in the United States and abroad, discusses the state-of-the-art in CB transplantation (CBT). We highlight recent outcome data from multiple domestic and international centers with CBT expertise, across both adult and pediatric settings. Applying these data, we outline 4 clinical scenarios where CB may be the graft of choice: patients who lack a suitable, young, readily available donor, those in need of urgent transplantation, patients with difficult-to-cure acute leukemia or myelodysplastic syndrome, and patients with non-malignant diseases. We also present potential mechanisms underlying the unique graft-versus-leukemia effects mediating reduced relapse following CBT, along with the advantages of reduced chronic GVHD. This position statement emphasizes the critical, ongoing role of CBT in the transplant field, and will help guide transplant physicians to consider CBT as a preferred donor (or, as needed, referral to a center with CBT expertise) for patients in these scenarios.

43033914.title: Real-world access and barriers to CAR T-cell therapy in relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a population-based study.
43033914.author: Li H
43033914.abstract:
BACKGROUND: CAR T-cell therapy has transformed outcomes of relapsed/refractory (R/R) diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), but access may be limited by clinical, geographic, logistical, and socioeconomic constraints. While <30% of eligible patients in the United States are estimated to receive CAR-T, little is known about population-level utilization and barriers to CAR-T within publicly funded healthcare systems such as Canada.
OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of patients with R/R DLBCL who were intended for and treated with CAR-T, to identify barriers to treatment, and to describe clinical outcomes.
STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective, population-based study included all adults diagnosed with DLBCL in 2023 and 2024 in the province of Alberta, Canada who subsequently initiated third-line or later (3L+) therapy at any time, or second-line therapy (2L) within 12 months of first-line treatment as of the approval of 2L CAR-T in November 2024. During this period, CAR-T was publicly funded through provincial health insurance and delivered at two referral centers in Calgary and Edmonton, serving a province of nearly 5 million people across 640,000 km². Patient support programs were available to reimburse travel expenses.
RESULTS: The study population comprised 93 patients who initiated 2L (n=51) or 3L+ (n=42) therapy for R/R DLBCL. Median age was 67 years (range 22-89), 67% were male, and 77% were married. Most (91%) lived in urban settings, with 23% residing >100km from a CAR-T center. In total, 67 (72%) patients were documented to be intended for CAR-T, of whom 65 (97%) underwent leukapheresis and 62 (93%) completed infusion. Failure to reach infusion was due to uncontrolled lymphoma (n=4) or patient decision (n=1). Objective response and complete response rates to CAR-T were 77% and 50%, respectively. Twelve-month progression-free survival (PFS) was 56% (95% CI 43-67%) and overall survival (OS) was 81% (95% CI 68-89%) among patients intended for CAR-T. There were 26 (28%) patients not intended for CAR-T due to uncontrolled lymphoma (n=12), advanced age/frailty (n=10), poor performance status (n=9), comorbidities (n=7), toxicity concerns (n=5), patient preference (n=4), unresolved complications from prior therapy (n=3), and/or psychosocial reasons (n=1). Geographic distance and marital status were not documented as barriers. Compared to those intended for CAR-T, these patients were older (median age 74 versus 64, p<0.0001) and more likely to have ECOG >1 (62% versus 25%, p=0.0016) and IPI score 3-5 (73% versus 48%, p=0.037). Non-CAR-T therapies included chemoimmunotherapy (n=10), an antibody-drug conjugate-based regimen (n=7), radiation (n=5), or bispecific antibodies (n=4). Twelve-month PFS and OS were 25% (95% CI 9-44%) and 30% (95% CI 11-51%), respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: A publicly funded provincial CAR-T program enabled approximately two-thirds of patients initiating 2L or 3L+ therapy for R/R DLBCL to access CAR-T with favorable real-world outcomes. Poor fitness and uncontrolled disease, rather than geographic or social factors, were the dominant barriers. Novel strategies are urgently needed for the minority of patients who do not receive CAR-T.

43026256.title: Bridging to CD19 CAR T-cell therapy for large B-cell lymphoma: An analysis of 1,134 patients by the EBMT Lymphoma Working Party and the GoCART Coalition.
43026256.author: Berning P
43026256.abstract: CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy (CAR T) is effective in relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (R/R LBCL), but the role of bridging therapy (BT) remains incompletely defined. We analyzed 1,134 patients with R/R LBCL treated with axicabtagene ciloleucel or tisagenlecleucel between 2018 and July 2023. BT was categorized as polatuzumab vedotin-bendamustine-rituximab (Pola-BR), low-dose regimens, classical salvage chemo-immunotherapy, or radiotherapy. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) from CAR T infusion were primary endpoints. Overall, 900 patients (79.5%) received BT and 232 (20.5%) did not (No-BT). At lymphodepletion, BT recipients more often had elevated LDH, bulky disease, and ECOG ≥2, yet had higher complete remission rates. Three-year PFS was 34.3% with BT versus 44.7% with No-BT, and OS was 44.4% versus 57.4%. In multivariable analyses, No-BT remained associated with superior OS (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.49-0.82) and PFS (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55-0.87). Improvement in disease status between apheresis and lymphodepletion occurred more often with BT and was associated with improved outcomes (3-year PFS 47.5% vs. 28.9 and 27.7% for stable/worsened disease among BT recipients). BT modality influenced conversion rates but not adjusted OS, PFS, or relapse. Our data suggest bridging therapy may prioritize disease control with minimal toxicity rather than any specific regimen.

43002421.title: Preclinical characterization of the potent and selective MALT1 inhibitor safimaltib in B-cell lymphoma models.
43002421.author: Philippar U
43002421.abstract: Constitutive activation of the B-cell receptor (BCR) pathway drives non-Hodgkin lymphomas. MALT1 is a key mediator of NF-κB signaling downstream of B- and T-cell receptors. Herein, we report development of safimaltib (JNJ-67856633), a selective, allosteric inhibitor of MALT1 protease. The crystal structure of safimaltib bound to MALT1 was determined, and enzyme kinetic studies were performed to characterize its inhibitory mechanism. Sub-micromolar doses of safimaltib inhibited growth of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) cell lines with activation of NF-κB signaling and models mimicking BTK inhibition resistance. Notably, activating mutations in BCR-pathway components were strongly associated with safimaltib response in vitro. Safimaltib demonstrated efficacy in DLBCL and MCL mouse models and synergy with a BTK inhibitor. Safimaltib was well tolerated in preclinical immunocompetent animal models with a safety profile supporting MALT1 targeting in humans. Overall, these results provide rationale for the first-in-human MALT1 inhibitor clinical trial.

43020917.title: Survival trends in Waldenström macroglobulinemia and comparison of outcomes with the general United States population.
43020917.author: Khan MA
43020917.abstract: Therapeutic options for Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) have expanded but improvements in overall-survival (OS) are difficult to interpret due to competing non-WM mortality. We conducted a large single-center retrospective study of 1020 patients with WM to evaluate survival trends. Patients were stratified by era of active WM diagnosis using a two-era model (1996-2005 and post-2006). OS did not differ significantly across eras in the overall cohort (p = 0.64). However, among patients aged <65 years at the time of active WM diagnosis, OS improved in the post-2006 era (median 18.8 vs. 14.1 years, p = 0.018). Cause-specific-survival (CSS) improved across eras, increasing from 15.6 years in 1996-2005 to 18.9 years post-2006 (p < 0.0001). Competing-risk-analysis (CRA) demonstrated a reduction in WM-related mortality over time (p < 0.001). However, excess mortality persisted, with a standardized mortality ratio (SMR) of 2.79 (p < 0.001) among patients <65 years compared with a matched U.S. population. Our findings highlight improvements in WM-specific survival, while gains in OS are observed in younger patients.

43031377.title: Caregiver support in patients with plasma cell dyscrasias: A novel single-item pilot measure of caregiver availability: Results from a survey of >1000 patients.
43031377.author: Mohyuddin GR
43031377.abstract: Treatment for plasma cell dyscrasias imposes burdens on patients and caregivers, particularly for cellular therapies. Traditional social determinants of health may not capture caregiver availability. We conducted a cross-sectional survey through HealthTree. Patients categorized their caregiver support through a single question: cohabiting dedicated caregiver, non-cohabiting dedicated caregiver, arrangeable support when needed or inadequate support. Among 1231 respondents, 68% had live-in caregivers, 3% had dedicated non-cohabiting caregivers, 23% arranged support when needed and 5% struggled to find support. Living arrangement had the strongest correlation with caregiver availability: 85% of married patients had live-in support compared to 6%-12% among divorced, widowed or never-married patients. Live-in caregiver support was lower in females than males (63% vs. 76%, respectively, p < 0.001), and in Black versus White patients (46% vs. 71%, respectively, p = 0.002). Employment, education level, distance from treatment centres and insurance type showed no association. Caregiver support for patients with plasma cell dyscrasias is primarily determined by household structure. Despite selection bias in our cohort, one-third of patients lacked dedicated caregiving assistance and 5% actively struggled to secure help. No single demographic variable reliably predicts caregiver availability, emphasizing the need for direct assessment as a standard question in clinical and research settings.

43033916.title: Invasive fungal infections after moderate or severe chronic graft-versus-host disease in allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant recipients: incidence, timing, and associated factors.
43033916.author: Rodriguez-Rodriguez S
43033916.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal infection (IFI) after moderate or severe chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGvHD) remains incompletely characterized in the setting of contemporary antifungal prophylaxis and immunosuppressive therapy.
OBJECTIVES: to estimate the incidence and timing of post-cGvHD IFI and identify clinical factors associated with IFI.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of consecutive allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation recipients with moderate or severe cGvHD requiring systemic therapy, diagnosed between 2010 and 2024. Cumulative incidence of IFI was estimated from cGvHD diagnosis, with death before IFI treated as a competing event. A prespecified Fine-Gray model evaluated transplant era, age at transplantation, donor type, conditioning intensity, and baseline cGvHD severity. Selected cGvHD treatments and antifungal prophylaxis were evaluated as active time-dependent exposures in separate cause-specific Cox models. An exploratory analysis was restricted to patients with severe cGvHD.
RESULTS: Among 388 patients with moderate or severe cGvHD, 56 (14.4%) developed post-cGvHD IFI. All observed IFIs were pulmonary and presented as invasive fungal pneumonia. Fifty-four infections were probable, and two were proven; invasive aspergillosis accounted for 89% (n=50) of cases. Cumulative incidence of IFI was 4.9%, 9.0%, and 11.6% at 6 months, 1 year, and 2 years, respectively, after cGvHD diagnosis. Baseline severe cGvHD (sHR 2.99 [95% CI 1.55-5.75], p=0.001) was associated with a higher risk of IFI, whereas a more recent transplant era was associated with a lower risk (sHR 0.59 [0.36-0.99], p=0.045). In the severe-cGvHD restricted analysis, lung cGvHD involvement (adjusted HR 4.99 [2.29-10.87], p<0.001) was associated with IFI. In exploratory time-dependent analyses, MMF (HR 3.87 [2.20-6.79], p<0.001) and prednisone exposure (HR 4.10 [1.89-8.89], p < 0.001) were associated with higher IFI risk.
CONCLUSION: Baseline severe cGvHD and lung cGvHD involvement were associated with higher subsequent IFI incidence. Prospective studies should evaluate risk-adapted mold-active prophylaxis using time-updated clinical and treatment factors in this population.

43025811.title: Model-informed precision dosing of busulfan in Adults: Real world implications for Dosing and Transplant outcomes.
43025811.author: Bracha L
43025811.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Busulfan has been a cornerstone of conditioning regimens for hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) for decades. Systemic busulfan exposure has been associated with clinical outcomes. Both underexposure and overexposure carry risks of relapse and graft failure on one hand, and toxicity or non-relapse mortality on the other. Model-informed precision dosing (MIPD), based on early pharmacokinetic measurements, has been introduced to optimize individual exposure and improve outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to evaluate the impact of MIPD on transplantation outcomes in adults treated at a large medical center.
STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included adult patients who underwent allogeneic HCT for malignant diseases between 1/1/2010 and 31/12/2022. Patients were divided into two groups based on the intravenous busulfan dosing strategy, a body weight-based dosing group (1/1/2010 to 31/12/2017) and a MIPD group (31/12/2017 to 31/12/2022). Busulfan plasma concentrations were measured after the first dose and analyzed using the NextDose platform to guide individualized dosing. The cumulative target AUC over 4 days was 79 mgh/L. Transplantation and disease related variables, toxicity (CTCAE grade 3-4 by day 100), and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) were recorded. Survival outcomes included overall survival (OS), event-free survival (EFS), GVHD-free relapse-free survival (GRFS), relapse-free survival (RFS), and non-relapse mortality (NRM). Multivariable logistic regression, Cox proportional hazards models, and competing risk analyses using Fine-Gray models were applied.
RESULTS: Among 107 patients, 62 received weight-based busulfan and 45 received MIPD. Baseline characteristics were largely comparable, although the MIPD group had a different ethnic distribution (p=0.007) and a lower Karnofsky score (p=0.024). Survival outcomes favored the MIPD group with OS (p=0.004), EFS (p=0.0053) and GRFS (p=0.0047). Higher conditioning intensity (dual alkylating agents) was associated with lower relapse in both groups (p=0.040, 0.011) and with improved OS only in the weight-based dosing group (p<0.001). Mucositis was more frequent with MIPD (p<0.001), and GVHD rates were similar between groups. In multivariable Cox regression analysis, MIPD (HR 0.40; p=0.009) and conditioning intensity (HR 0.37; p=0.003) were independently associated with improved OS. Competing risk analysis showed significantly lower non-relapse mortality in the MIPD group (p=0.009), but no significant difference in relapse probability (p=0.44).
CONCLUSIONS: Our study compared weight-based dosing and MIPD of busulfan in adults undergoing allogeneic HCT. Transplantation outcomes were improved due to reduced mortality in the busulfan MIPD cohort. These finding highlight the potential of individualized dosing strategies to improve the therapeutic balance in transplantation.

43020330.title: Severe graft-versus-host disease and limited durable response with mogamulizumab for post-transplant relapse of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
43020330.author: Fujita S
43020330.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The safety and efficacy of mogamulizumab (MOG) for post-transplant relapse of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL) remain uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: We investigated the clinical outcomes of MOG therapy, with particular attention to graft-versus-host disease and antitumor efficacy, in patients with post-transplant relapsed ATL.
STUDY DESIGN: We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients who received MOG for post-transplant relapsed ATL at a single center.
RESULTS: Thirty-three consecutive patients received MOG for post-transplant relapsed ATL. The median interval from allo-HCT to MOG initiation was 104 days. The cumulative incidence of grade II-IV acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) by day 100 after MOG initiation was 55.8%, including grade III-IV acute GVHD in 34.2% of patients. Severe acute GVHD developed irrespective of the interval between transplantation and MOG initiation. Exploratory analyses identified unrelated peripheral blood stem cell transplantation and lower soluble interleukin-2 receptor levels at MOG initiation as factors associated with grade III-IV acute GVHD. The overall response rate was 61%, including complete remission in 39% of patients, with the highest response observed in peripheral blood disease. However, relapse or disease progression occurred in 15 of the 20 responders. The median overall survival (OS) from MOG initiation was 6.9 months, with 1- and 2-year OS rates of 40.6% and 21.9%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: MOG demonstrated clinically meaningful short-term antitumor activity in patients with post-transplant relapsed ATL, particularly in peripheral blood disease, but was associated with a substantial risk of severe acute GVHD and limited durable disease control. Careful patient selection and rational sequential or combination treatment strategies are warranted to optimize MOG use after allo-HCT.

43014545.title: Association of Post-Transplant Cyclophosphamide Dose with BK Virus-Associated Hemorrhagic Cystitis after Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation.
43014545.author: Yae H
43014545.abstract:
BACKGROUND: BK virus-associated hemorrhagic cystitis (BK-HC) is a common complication of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT). Although post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) is associated with an increased risk of BK-HC, the impact of PTCy dose remains unclear. In addition, the roles of conditioning-related urothelial injury and early post-transplant inflammation in BK-HC development in the PTCy era have not been fully elucidated.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association between total PTCy dose and BK-HC incidence and to identify clinical risk factors for BK-HC, with a particular focus on conditioning regimens and early post-transplant inflammatory complications.
STUDY DESIGN: We retrospectively analyzed 380 consecutive patients who underwent allo-HCT at our institution between January 2015 and July 2024. The cumulative incidence and risk factors for BK-HC were evaluated in the overall cohort, followed by subgroup analyses according to PTCy use.
RESULTS: Of the 380 patients, 180 received PTCy (88% with peripheral blood stem cell grafts) at total doses of 50 mg/kg (n = 40), 75 mg/kg (n = 35), and 100 mg/kg (n = 105). Grade 2-4 BK-HC developed in 46 patients at a median of 37 days (range, 10-106 days) after transplantation. The 1-year cumulative incidence of BK-HC was significantly higher in patients receiving PTCy than in those who did not (17.5% vs. 7.6%, P < .01). In the overall cohort, the 1-year cumulative incidence increased across the 0, 50, 75, and 100 mg/kg PTCy dose groups (7.6%, 10.5%, 17.3%, and 20.1%, respectively; P for trend < .01). PTCy and high-dose corticosteroid use were independently associated with BK-HC. Among PTCy recipients, busulfan-containing conditioning and high-dose corticosteroid use remained independent risk factors. Furthermore, patients with busulfan exposure or grade ≥ 2 cytokine release syndrome exhibited a significantly higher incidence of BK-HC.
CONCLUSION: In this single-center retrospective cohort with evolving institutional transplant practices, BK-HC incidence was numerically higher across the 0, 50, 75, and 100 mg/kg PTCy dose groups. Among PTCy recipients, busulfan-containing conditioning and high-dose corticosteroid use further increased this risk, whereas early post-transplant cytokine release syndrome may serve as a clinical marker for identifying patients at a particularly high risk of subsequent BK-HC.

43020332.title: Ligand/receptor-based chimeric antigen receptors: a promising alternative to conventional scFv designs in cancer immunotherapy.
43020332.author: Yumashev A
43020332.abstract: Engineering immune cells, particularly T lymphocytes, with chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) has become one of the most successful modalities of cancer immunotherapy, as evidenced by the approval and clinical use of multiple CAR-T cell products. Current CAR platforms predominantly rely on monoclonal antibody-derived single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) for target recognition. While scFv-based CARs have achieved remarkable clinical successes, they also exhibit notable limitations, including the potential to elicit anti-CAR immune responses, tonic signaling that contributes to CAR-T cell exhaustion, tumor escape via antigen loss or downregulation, and on-target, off-tumor toxicities. In response, researchers have explored alternative binding moieties for CAR architectures. Natural ligands and receptors represent one such class of alternatives. These approaches may offer advantages over conventional scFv-based CARs, such as potentially lower immunogenicity with fully human-derived domains, the ability to engage multiple targets or ligands, access to antigens that are challenging for scFvs, and the use of protein-protein interfaces shaped by evolution within human physiology. However, these benefits are not absolute. CAR junctions, non-native orientations, expression levels, modifications, and the cellular context can still generate immunogenic epitopes or dysfunctional products. Additionally, natural ligand/receptor pairs may transmit unwanted agonistic or regulatory signals that require careful engineering to mitigate. This review discusses recent advances in ligand/receptor-based CARs from a translational perspective. It also provides a critical overview of their inherent limitations, alongside potential solutions to support the rational design of next-generation constructs.

43014547.title: Traversing the Last Mile: Bringing Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell Therapy to the Community Setting.
43014547.author: Majhail NS
43014547.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed treatment of hematologic malignancies, yet access remains limited by geographic, referral, infrastructure, and treatment-center capacity barriers. Expanding CAR T-cell therapy into community oncology settings offers an opportunity to increase capacity and provide treatment closer to where patients live. Drawing on the experience of a community-based transplant and cellular therapy network, we propose a practical framework for establishing community-based CAR T-cell therapy programs. Program development should begin with market and gap assessments to define patient need, existing capabilities, infrastructure requirements, and financial sustainability. Foundational elements include multidisciplinary clinical and administrative leadership, trained personnel, appropriate outpatient and infusion space, and solutions for apheresis, product storage, and logistics. Standardized clinical pathways, staff training, electronic health record-enabled workflows, and operating procedures are essential for patient selection, treatment delivery, toxicity management, and care coordination. Outpatient care requires structured monitoring, rapid escalation pathways, and an engaged hospital partner for emergency and inpatient management of complications. Programs must also establish capabilities for payer and manufacturer contracting, revenue-cycle management, regulatory requirements, and management of out-of-specification products. Robust quality systems and continuous quality improvement are fundamental to developing safe, sustainable, high-quality community CAR T-cell programs.
